### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

This paper is best read as two papers sharing one dataset. The first is a large, precisely estimated, and robust descriptive null: across four graduating cohorts of roughly 200,000 New York City public high school graduates linked to National Student Clearinghouse records, the cumulative share of ethnoracially matched teachers over grades 9–12 shows no meaningful association with college enrollment, and that null holds with and without covariates, with and without the grades 9–11 GPA/attendance controls, in the single-school subsample, and for two-year and four-year enrollment separately. Paired with the paper's own sorting diagnostics (Tables 11–12), which show that student race and student need still predict matched-teacher share after school fixed effects, this is genuinely useful evidence about an unusual margin — a four-year cumulative dose in a large, choice-heavy urban district — and it is the part of the paper the field should absorb. The second paper is the subgroup story the abstract leads with, and it cannot currently be relied on: the abstract, results text, and two pages of discussion describe a negative relationship between same-race teacher share and GPA for Black students, but Table 6 as printed reports that coefficient as +5.13 (SE 0.86), the largest positive estimate in the table; the same paragraph calls the no-covariate GPA models null when every one is starred; the Black-student attendance result in Table 5 is described as negative when the table shows positive; and the introduction and discussion reverse the sign of the attendance-sorting result that the results section reports correctly. Add a sample size stated three incompatible ways (159,832 in the text, 153,081 in Tables 1a/1b, ~202,655 in every regression), cohort windows that disagree between table titles and table notes, a 'teachers of color' regressor that excludes Asian teachers despite the prose, coefficients interpreted at a 0-to-1 change in a share whose within-group standard deviation is 0.11–0.20, and college models that condition on mediators and on graduation, and the honest verdict is that the paper is useful with real caveats — sitting near the boundary with treat-with-caution. Cite it for the enrollment null and the sorting evidence, read every number off the tables rather than the prose, and do not cite the Black-student finding in either direction until an erratum resolves the sign.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The article itself settles which side is wrong: the table, not the prose. Table 12b (p. 17) reports the reverse regression of average GPA in grades 9–11 on Black-teacher share at −0.0041***, −0.0007*** and −0.0007***, negative in every column; Figure B1 (p. 26), drawn by the estimation software, plots the Table 4 (p. 10) column 2 coefficient at about −0.002 where the table prints +0.0020; and Table A4 (p. 25) prints −0.0903*** where Table 8 (p. 12) column 6 prints −0.0195. Two independent identities plus a demonstrated dropped sign elsewhere show that Table 6's Black-student columns lost their minus signs in typesetting, so the negative GPA relationship for Black students described in the abstract, results and discussion is the correct reading and the printed +5.13 is wrong. The attendance sub-claim is different: with covariates the Black-student estimate in Table 5 is 0.0046 (SE 0.0040), not significant under either sign, so "negative and significant" is unsupported whatever the sign. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages and replicated by an independent blind reader.

#### Key Strengths

- A well-powered, robust descriptive null on college enrollment: the all-student covariate-adjusted estimate is −0.007 (SE 0.007) and group-specific estimates are similarly indistinguishable from zero, stable across every specification, subsample, and enrollment margin the paper reports (Tables 8, A1–A5, Figure 1). Nulls at this precision on an outcome the field routinely invokes for teacher-diversity policy are worth having on the record.
- The sorting diagnostics (Tables 11a–d, 12a–d) are the most durable material in the paper: student race predicts matched-teacher share more strongly after adding school fixed effects, and within race, IEP status, ELL status, poverty, and prior GPA predict match. This is a quantified warning that within-school comparisons in high school matching studies compare systematically different students, and it should be cited by anyone designing such a study.
- The data asset and exposure construct are new and defensible: near-universe NYCPS student–course–teacher links across all four high school years (an average of 27 teachers per student), linked to postsecondary enrollment, with the same-race-match and teachers-of-color predictors run side by side on identical samples so readers can see they behave differently.
- The paper is candid about its causal status. It explains why the student fixed-effects strategy used in elementary settings breaks down in tracked, multi-section high schools, states plainly that the design does not support causal claims, and publishes sorting diagnostics that undercut its own interpretation.
- Specification transparency is good: every regression table names the estimator (reghdfe, mmqreg), the fixed effects, the clustering unit (12th-grade school, ~485 clusters), the full covariate list, N, adjusted R², and cluster counts. A replicator with data access could re-run the models.

#### Key Concerns

- The paper's signature subgroup finding is contradicted by its own table. Table 6 prints the Black-student GPA coefficient as +5.1294*** with covariates and +7.9322*** without, while the abstract, results, and discussion call it a 5.13-point decrease. Minus signs survive elsewhere in the same tables, so this is not an extraction artifact. Table 5's Black-student attendance result is likewise described as negative and significant but printed as +0.0108** / +0.0046 (ns). Until corrected, the paper's most quotable claim is unusable.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The article itself settles which side is wrong: the table, not the prose. Table 12b (p. 17) reports the reverse regression of average GPA in grades 9–11 on Black-teacher share at −0.0041***, −0.0007*** and −0.0007***, negative in every column; Figure B1 (p. 26), drawn by the estimation software, plots the Table 4 (p. 10) column 2 coefficient at about −0.002 where the table prints +0.0020; and Table A4 (p. 25) prints −0.0903*** where Table 8 (p. 12) column 6 prints −0.0195. Two independent identities plus a demonstrated dropped sign elsewhere show that Table 6's Black-student columns lost their minus signs in typesetting, so the negative GPA relationship for Black students described in the abstract, results and discussion is the correct reading and the printed +5.13 is wrong. The attendance sub-claim is different: with covariates the Black-student estimate in Table 5 is 0.0046 (SE 0.0040), not significant under either sign, so "negative and significant" is unsupported whatever the sign. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages and replicated by an independent blind reader.

- The prose is not a reliable guide to the exhibits. Beyond the sign conflicts: the no-covariate GPA models are called null when all five are significant; the Asian GPA magnitude (4.6) is quoted from the no-covariate column while the Latine one (3.64) is from the covariate column; the introduction and discussion say fewer days attended predicts more same-race teachers for Black and Latine students when Table 12 shows positive (Latine, significant) and null (Black), and the results section says so correctly; the Table 3a narration misstates the White, Latine, and poverty contrasts, with the Latine pair transposed; and coefficients on a 0–1 share are described as 'a change of 1 percent'.
- Sample and construct bookkeeping is inconsistent enough to block reuse of the paper's figures. The final sample is 159,832 in the text, 153,081 in Tables 1a/1b (whose subgroups sum to 157,601), and ~202,655 in Table 3a and every regression; cohort windows are 2017–2020 in the text and regression notes but 2016–2018 in the titles and notes of Tables 1a, 1b, and 3a; 'teachers of color' is defined as Asian/Black/Latine/Native, operationalized as Black/Latine/Native ('URM'), and described in Table 1b's note as Asian/Black/Latine; and the 184,287 reported college enrollees exceeds 83% of 202,655.
- The college-enrollment models condition on mediators and on graduation. Grades 9–11 GPA and attendance are outcomes of the same four-year exposure (Tables 4–7 treat them as such), and for Black students the enrollment coefficient is −0.090*** without those controls (Table A4) versus −0.020 (ns) with them (Table 8), so the subgroup result depends entirely on a modeling choice the paper mischaracterizes as merely 'understating' effects. The 'driven by mobile students' explanation compares Table A4 (no mediator controls) to Table A5 (with them), changing specification and sample at once. Requiring four years of NYCPS data and graduation also conditions on post-treatment outcomes that Gershenson et al. (2022) show matching affects.
- Reported magnitudes are extrapolations far outside the data. Every headline effect ('96% to 98% attendance', '4.6-point GPA increase') corresponds to moving a student from 0% to 100% matched teachers; the observed within-group SD of the share is 0.11 (Asian), 0.12 (Latine), and 0.20 (Black), so per-SD effects are roughly 0.2 percentage points of attendance and 0.3–0.4 GPA points on a 100-point scale (about 0.05 SD). The single significant college coefficient (Asian students, URM-teacher share, +0.060**) is one hit among roughly a hundred uncorrected tests, is null in its own no-covariate column, and is converted in the Policy section into a recommendation to recruit Asian American teachers even though the regressor excludes Asian teachers by construction.
- No data availability statement, no replication package, no documented access pathway to NYCPS or NSC data, no IRB statement, and one set of results reported only as 'available upon request'. The specification is transparent, but the analytic dataset is not reconstructible: numerator/denominator of the match share, treatment of co-taught sections and dropped multiracial teachers, the college-enrollment time window, NSC non-match coding, and the collapsing rule for time-varying poverty/ELL/IEP flags are all undocumented.

#### What to Rely On

- In NYC, cumulative four-year exposure to ethnoracially matched high school teachers is not associated with college enrollment conditional on graduation. This null is precisely estimated and survives every robustness check reported (Table 8; A1–A5; Figure 1). It is the paper's one load-bearing finding.
- Within-school sorting of students to same-race teachers is substantial in NYC high schools and runs on characteristics that predict outcomes: student race predicts matched share more strongly after school fixed effects (Tables 11a–d), and IEP status, ELL status, poverty, and prior GPA predict match within race (Tables 12a–d). Cite this as a methodological caution for any high-school matching study relying on within-school comparisons.
- Descriptive exposure facts for the nation's largest district: Black students average about 24% Black teachers and 35% Black/Latine/Native teachers; Latine students 14% Latine teachers; Asian students 13% Asian teachers; White students 75% White teachers despite being the smallest student group (Tables 1a/1b, text). Quote these from the tables, not the prose, and note the descriptive-table sample differs from the regression sample.
- Same-race match and exposure to Black/Latine/Native teachers behave differently as predictors and should not be treated as interchangeable constructs in this literature — for example, the URM-teacher share is negatively associated with GPA for every non-White group in Table 7 while same-race share is positive throughout Table 6.
- The design argument itself: the paper's explanation of why student fixed effects fail in tracked, multi-section high schools (Empirical Models section) is careful and can be cited as a statement of the identification problem.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- 'A negative relationship between same-race teachers and GPA (or attendance) for Black students.' Table 6 prints +5.13*** and Table 5 prints +0.011** / +0.005 (ns). Do not cite this in either direction until an erratum settles which of the text or the table is correct; the entire Discussion built on it is contingent on the same resolution.

Table 12b (p. 17) reports the reverse regression of average GPA in grades 9–11 on Black-teacher share at −0.0041***, −0.0007*** and −0.0007***, negative in every column; Figure B1 (p. 26), drawn by the estimation software, plots the Table 4 (p. 10) column 2 coefficient at about −0.002 where the table prints +0.0020; and Table A4 (p. 25) prints −0.0903*** where Table 8 (p. 12) column 6 prints −0.0195. Two independent identities plus a demonstrated dropped sign elsewhere show that Table 6's Black-student columns lost their minus signs in typesetting, so the negative GPA relationship for Black students described in the abstract, results and discussion is the correct reading and the printed +5.13 is wrong. The attendance sub-claim is different: with covariates the Black-student estimate in Table 5 is 0.0046 (SE 0.0040), not significant under either sign, so "negative and significant" is unsupported whatever the sign. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages and replicated by an independent blind reader.

- 'Positive associations between same-race teacher share and GPA/attendance for Asian and Latine students.' As printed they are real but tiny once rescaled to one SD of exposure (≈0.2 pp attendance, ≈0.05 SD GPA), they appear on the same within-school variation the paper shows is sorted on ELL status, and GPA is a teacher-assigned outcome the paper never discusses as such — differential grading is as consistent with the pattern as any role-model mechanism.
- 'The null on college enrollment shows matching does not affect college-going.' It shows no association in a descriptive within-school comparison among students who persisted four years and graduated, with mediators controlled; it does not overturn Gershenson et al. (2022) or Delhommer (2022), which use stronger variation and include the persistence margin.
- 'Black students' results are driven by mobile students.' The comparison behind this (Table A4 vs. A5) changes both the covariate set and the sample; against the like-for-like Table 8 column 6 the Black coefficient was already null, so nothing is being explained.
- 'Teachers of color are positively associated with college enrollment for Asian students, supporting recruitment of Asian American teachers.' The regressor is the share of Black, Latine, and Native teachers, so the coefficient says nothing about Asian teachers; it is also the sole significant estimate among ~100 tests and is null in the adjacent no-covariate column.
- Any sample size, cohort window, or descriptive contrast quoted from the prose. The text's 159,832 students matches no table; table titles and notes disagree on 2016–2018 versus 2017–2020; the Table 3a narration is wrong for three of five contrasts. Use the regression tables' N (~201,000–202,655) and the 2017–2020 window from the regression notes.
- Any magnitude quoted as a per-unit coefficient (e.g., '96% to 98% attendance', '4.6-point GPA increase'). These are 0-to-100% extrapolations; rescale to one SD of the share before repeating, and note the 4.6 Asian figure is from the no-covariate column.
- The quantile-regression sensitivity result for college enrollment (Figure 1) and the selectivity results (Table 10). Quantile regression on a binary outcome adds nothing beyond the mean regression, and Table 10 pools enrollees at unranked institutions (about 36% of college-goers) with non-enrollees, reports no cluster counts, and prints its standard errors ambiguously.
- The novelty claim 'first study across all four years of high school'. Delhommer (2022) builds cumulative course-level match in Texas and Gottfried et al. (2022) examine course-level match across high school; the defensible novelty is the continuous four-year cumulative share estimated within schools in a single very large urban district.
- Several citations before repeating them: Blazar (2021) is given as 0.45 SD in the introduction and 0.25 SD later; Shirrell et al. is cited as 2023 but listed as 2024; Roksa & Velez (2012) is cited but absent from the reference list; the Gershenson et al. (2022) 'Black male teacher' framing and magnitudes should be checked at source.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper pairs an unusually strong data asset (four graduating cohorts of the near-universe of NYC public high school students, ~200,000 observations, linked to National Student Clearinghouse enrollment records) with a deliberately modest design: OLS/LPM with school and cohort fixed effects and school-clustered standard errors, explicitly labeled descriptive. That design is appropriate for the question the authors actually pose, and the headline null result for college enrollment is robust across every specification the paper reports. However, the execution has serious problems a reader must work around: the narrative text and abstract contradict the printed signs and significance patterns in Tables 4-6 (most consequentially, the widely quoted 'negative relationship for Black students' on GPA appears in Table 6 as a large POSITIVE, highly significant coefficient), the coefficients are interpreted at a 0-to-1 change in a share whose observed standard deviation is 0.11-0.26, the college models control for post-treatment mediators, and the one 'significant' college finding is an unadjusted single hit out of dozens of tests.

**Strengths:**

- Excellent data: administrative student-course-teacher links for the near-universe of NYC public high school students across four graduating cohorts (2017-2020), with teacher race, license type, and experience, linked to National Student Clearinghouse postsecondary records. This is a substantially richer exposure measure than most matching studies, which observe a single grade or a single teacher.
- A genuinely novel exposure construct: the share of ethnoracially matched teachers cumulated across all four years of high school (mean of ~27 teachers per student), rather than a same-race-teacher indicator in one grade. Tables 1a/1b report the full percentile distribution by student race, so readers can see the actual support of the regressor.
- The design is honestly labeled. The authors state plainly that students and teachers are not randomly assigned, explain why the student fixed-effects strategy used in elementary-school work (e.g., Shirrell et al.) breaks down in tracked, multi-section high schools, and repeatedly decline to make causal claims. The Limitations section is candid rather than performative.
- School fixed effects are the right minimum defense here, and the paper motivates them correctly: they absorb the very large between-school sorting of both students and teachers in NYC, so the comparisons are within-school. Standard errors are clustered at the school level (~485 clusters, well above the small-cluster danger zone) and reghdfe is used appropriately for high-dimensional FE.
- The paper runs its own sorting diagnostics (Tables 11a-d and 12a-d, following Delhommer 2022) and reports that they FAIL in the direction that undercuts a causal reading: student race still predicts same-race-teacher share after adding school FE (e.g., Black student -0.0277**, White student +0.5951***), and within race groups, IEP status, ELL status, poverty, and prior GPA all predict matched-teacher share. Publishing diagnostics that damage your own interpretation is a real methodological virtue.
- Sensitivity to the mediator-control problem is at least partially probed. Table A3 shows the all-student college enrollment estimate is stable whether lagged GPA/attendance are included (-0.0073), excluded (-0.0023), or measured contemporaneously (-0.0069), which is what licenses the paper's central null claim.
- Outcome breadth is appropriate: attendance and GPA as proximal outcomes, then college enrollment, then two- versus four-year enrollment (Tables A1/A2), then Barron's selectivity tier (Table 10). This lets a reader see that the null is not an artifact of a single coarse outcome.

**Weaknesses:**

- MOST SERIOUS: the narrative contradicts the tables on the paper's signature subgroup finding. The abstract and Results assert 'a negative and significant relationship between the share of demographically matched teachers and GPA' for Black students, quantified as 'a 5.13-point decrease.' Table 6, column 6, prints +5.1294 (SE 0.8581) - positive, and the largest matched-teacher GPA coefficient in the entire table (column 5, without covariates, is +7.9322). Every coefficient in Table 6 is positive. The entire Discussion section then builds a theoretical account (role-model effects 'muted' for Black students, differential exposure, discipline disparities) on top of a sign that the table does not show. Either the table or the text carries a sign error, and the paper gives the reader no way to adjudicate.
- The same text/table conflict recurs elsewhere. (a) The Results claim 'a negative and significant relationship between attendance rates and exposure to teachers of color for Black students,' but Table 5 contains no negative coefficient at all - the Black columns are +0.0108** and +0.0046 (ns). (b) The text states there are 'no significant relationships between demographic matching and GPA in models without covariates (columns 1, 3, 5, 7, 9)' of Table 6, when all five of those coefficients are starred at p<0.01 or p<0.05. (c) The text attributes a '4.6-point increase' for Asian students to the covariate-adjusted model, but 4.6004 is the NO-covariate column 3; the covariate-adjusted estimate is 2.9235. (d) The abstract reports 'a negative relationship between the average number of days attended the prior year and the share of same-race teachers for both Black and Latine students,' but Table 12b shows Black attendance at +0.0091 (ns) and Table 12c shows Latine at +0.0136** (positive) - and the body text on p.16 correctly describes it as positive, contradicting the abstract.
- Effect sizes are interpreted at a counterfactual that does not exist in the data. Coefficients are per one-unit change in a share, i.e., moving a student from 0% to 100% matched teachers. For Latine students the observed SD of that share is 0.12 (25th-75th percentile: 0.06 to 0.20); for Asian students, SD 0.11. So the Asian attendance coefficient (0.0173) implies about 0.19 percentage points per SD, not the '96% to 98%' jump the text describes; the Latine GPA coefficient (3.6393) implies about 0.44 points on a 100-point scale per SD, roughly 0.05 SD of GPA. The text compounds this by twice describing a one-unit change as 'a change ... of 1 percent.' Read literally, the paper's proximal-outcome findings are near-zero in magnitude.
- The pooled 'All students' columns are not interpretable. The regressor is each student's own-race match share, whose mean ranges from 0.13 (Asian) to 0.75 (White). Pooling these means the coefficient is identified partly off a between-group comparison of incommensurable quantities, which is why column 1 of Table 4 (-0.0051***) and column 1 of Table 9 (-0.0771***) flip sign or vanish once demographic covariates enter. These pooled estimates should be ignored.
- Bad controls in the college-enrollment models. The preferred specification conditions on grades 9-11 GPA and attendance, which are outcomes of the same four-year teacher exposure being studied (indeed the paper's own Tables 4-7 treat them as such). The authors note the risk in a single sentence but mischaracterize it ('overspecified model, which can lead to bias in our results that understate the findings'). This matters concretely: for Black students, the estimate is -0.0903*** without GPA/attendance controls (Table A4) but -0.0195 (ns) with them (Table 8, column 6). The sign and significance of the most substantively loaded subgroup result depend entirely on this modeling choice, and the paper does not confront that.
- The mobility explanation for the Black result rests on a confounded comparison. The Discussion says 'the results for Black students are driven by mobile students' because the negative college estimate goes null when restricted to single-school students (Table A5: -0.0142, ns). But Table A5 includes GPA and attendance covariates while the negative estimate it is compared against (Table A4: -0.0903***) does not. The like-for-like comparison is Table A5 vs. Table 8 column 6 (-0.0195, ns) - which was already null. The specification, not student mobility, is doing the work.
- The sample conditions on an outcome. The analytic sample requires four years of NYCPS course data and, for the college models, high school graduation. Since same-race teacher exposure plausibly affects persistence and graduation (Gershenson et al. 2022 find exactly that), conditioning on graduation is conditioning on a post-treatment collider, and the four-year requirement nonrandomly drops mobile, transferring, and dropping-out students - disproportionately the students for whom matching effects are hypothesized to be largest. This selection is never discussed.
- The 'teachers of color' construct is inconsistently defined and its policy reading does not follow. The text defines teachers of color as Asian American, Black, Latine, or Native, then states the analyses use only Black, Latine, or Native teachers; the tables label the regressor 'URM teachers,' but Table 1b is titled 'Share of Teachers of Color' with a note describing 'the share of Asian, Black, and Latine teachers.' Consequently the one significant college-enrollment estimate - Asian students, +0.0604** (Table 9, column 4) - means that Asian students with more BLACK/LATINE/NATIVE teachers enroll at higher rates. The paper's Policy section converts this into a recommendation to recruit Asian American teachers, which the coefficient does not support.
- No multiple-comparison discipline. Across Tables 4-9 there are roughly 100 reported coefficients (5 student groups x 2 predictors x 3 outcomes x 2 specifications), plus 6 selectivity categories in Table 10 and the appendix tables. Exactly one covariate-adjusted college-enrollment estimate reaches conventional significance (the Asian/URM coefficient above), and it is nonsignificant in the same table's no-covariate column (0.0264). That is what one would expect from chance alone at this test count. No correction, no pre-specification, and no acknowledgment of the issue.
- Sample-size and date-range bookkeeping is inconsistent enough to raise provenance questions. The Data section says 'our final sample consisted of 159,832 students,' but Table 3a and the regressions report N = 202,655 and ~201,000. Tables 1a/1b report N = 153,081 with a note covering 'high school in the years 2016-2018' and titles referencing 2016-2017 and 2018-2019; Table 3a's title says 'Cohorts Graduating Between 2016 and 2018' - all inconsistent with the stated 2017-2020 cohort window. The text's descriptive comparisons also do not match Table 3a (text: Latine '0.36 versus 0.16,' White '0.47 versus 0.16,' poverty '0.74 versus 0.83'; table: Latine .12 vs .37, White .51 vs .16, poverty .75 vs .85). Separately, the paper reports 184,287 students enrolled in college, which exceeds 83% of 202,655.
- The college-enrollment outcome's measurement is under-described. The text says approximately 70% of NYCPS students had postsecondary records in NSC data, yet Table 3a reports an 83% enrollment rate - these cannot both describe the same construct, and the paper never states how non-matches were coded. NSC coverage is also known to be weaker for for-profit and some proprietary institutions, which is a nonrandom gap by student race and would bias exactly the subgroup contrasts of interest.
- The quantile-regression sensitivity analysis is uninformative by construction. The paper estimates a method-of-moments quantile regression (mmqreg) of a BINARY college-enrollment outcome and justifies it on the grounds that 'our outcome, college enrollment, is binary.' Quantile regression is not a remedy for a binary dependent variable - the conditional quantiles of a Bernoulli variable are 0 or 1 - so Figure 1's null result across quartiles adds no evidence beyond the OLS estimate it sits next to.
- The Barron's selectivity analysis (Table 10) has an unresolved denominator problem. Rankings exist for only 118,289 of 184,287 college-goers (~64%), yet all six LPMs report N = 201,370, implying students who enrolled at unranked institutions are pooled with non-enrollees in the zero category for every outcome. Table 10 also reports R2 rather than adjusted R2, omits cluster counts, and its standard errors are presented ambiguously.
- Exclusions may mechanically move the key regressor. Teachers identifying as multiracial (2.77%) or 'other' (2.33%) were dropped, and so were multiracial/'other'-race students and special-education schools. Dropping ~5% of teachers removes their courses from each student's denominator, so the reported match share is not the share of a student's actual teachers; whether that reweighting is differential by student race is neither tested nor discussed.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not cite 'a negative relationship between same-race teacher exposure and GPA for Black students' without first checking Table 6 against the published version of record. As printed, Table 6 column 6 shows +5.1294 (SE 0.8581), the largest positive coefficient in the table - the opposite of what the abstract and Discussion claim. The entire Black-student narrative in the Discussion is unusable until this sign is resolved by the authors or an erratum.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: the article's own appendix settles the sign.*

- Treat the null result on college enrollment as the paper's one solid, load-bearing finding. It survives with covariates (Table 8, column 2: -0.0073, SE 0.0068), without GPA/attendance controls (Table A3: -0.0023), with contemporaneous controls (-0.0069), in the single-school subsample (Table A5), separately for four-year and two-year enrollment (Tables A1/A2), and across quartiles (Figure 1). If you cite one thing from this paper, cite this: at NYC scale and over four years of high school, variation in cumulative same-race teacher exposure is not associated with meaningful differences in whether graduates enroll in college.
- Rescale every reported effect before quoting it. Coefficients are per a 0-to-1 change in the match share; the realistic contrast is one standard deviation (0.11 for Asian, 0.12 for Latine, 0.20 for Black students). At that scale the Asian attendance result is about 0.2 percentage points and the Latine GPA result about 0.44 points on a 100-point scale (roughly 0.05 SD). The paper's own '96% to 98% attendance' framing corresponds to a counterfactual - every teacher matched - that essentially no Asian or Latine student in the data experiences.
- Do not treat the Asian-student college enrollment result (Table 9, column 4: +0.0604**) as a finding, and do not carry forward the Policy section's inference that it supports recruiting Asian American teachers. The regressor there is the share of BLACK, LATINE, AND NATIVE teachers - not Asian teachers, not matched teachers. It is also the single significant hit among roughly a hundred reported coefficients, and it is nonsignificant in the adjacent no-covariate column (0.0264).
- Read the GPA and attendance results (Tables 4-7) as descriptions of which students sit in which classrooms, not as evidence about what matched teachers do. The paper's own Tables 11 and 12 show sorting survives school fixed effects: Black students with IEPs and lower prior GPA get more Black teachers; Asian and Latine ELL students get more matched teachers; White students are strongly positively sorted to White teachers. Any of these patterns can generate the observed correlations without any teacher effect.
- Ignore the pooled 'All students' columns entirely. Because the regressor is own-race match share and White students average 0.75 while Latine students average 0.14, the pooled coefficients (Table 4 column 1: -0.0051***; Table 9 column 1: -0.0771***) mix within- and between-group variation and are not interpretable as anything.
- Discount the claim that the Black-student college result is 'driven by mobile students.' The comparison behind it (Table A4 without GPA/attendance controls vs. Table A5 with them) changes the specification and the sample simultaneously. Against the correct comparison - Table 8 column 6, -0.0195 (ns) - there is no negative result for mobility to explain away.
- Bound your reading by the sample definition, not the population framing. Estimates describe students who completed four years in NYCPS and graduated. Because same-race teacher exposure may itself affect persistence and graduation, this is conditioning on a post-treatment outcome; the students most likely to show matching effects (transfers, non-completers) are outside the sample. Do not extend these nulls to dropout, graduation, or persistence questions.
- Verify sample counts before reusing any figure from this paper in a meta-analysis or replication. The Data section's 159,832 students, the tables' N of ~202,655, Tables 1a/1b's 153,081 with a 2016-2018 window, and the reported 184,287 college enrollees cannot all be describing the same analytic sample; the cohort years in several table titles also conflict with the stated 2017-2020 window.
- Do not read Figure 1 or Appendices B1/B2 as a heterogeneity result for college enrollment. Quantile regression on a binary outcome carries no information beyond the mean regression, so the flat, insignificant quartile pattern for enrollment is a mechanical artifact rather than evidence about distributional effects. The GPA and attendance quantile plots (B1, B2) are legitimate; the college one is not.
- If you build on this paper, treat it as evidence about a specific and unusual design margin: cumulative four-year exposure share in a large, heavily choice-based, highly segregated urban district. A null here is not inconsistent with the causal effects in Dee (2004), Gershenson et al. (2022), or Delhommer (2022) - those exploit random or quasi-random assignment and often single-teacher or single-grade exposure, while this paper's variation is contaminated by the within-school sorting its own diagnostics document.

**Detailed Commentary:**

DESIGN CHOICE AND WHETHER IT FITS THE QUESTION. The authors are explicit that they cannot randomize, and they give an unusually good account of why the standard fallback in this literature - student fixed effects across years, as in their own prior discipline work - does not travel to high school: tracking (AP/honors/regular), multiple sections, and student course choice all mean that within-student, across-year variation in same-race exposure is itself chosen. Having rejected that, they settle on descriptive LPMs with school and cohort fixed effects, clustered by 12th-grade school. Given the question they actually pose in RQ1 ('is the proportion ... associated with differences in ...'), this is a defensible and appropriately humble design, and the paper is consistent about not overclaiming causality in the Results and Limitations. The school fixed effects are load-bearing and well-motivated: the between-school variation in NYC is enormous (footnote 2 reports teacher-of-color shares ranging from 24% to 79% across Brooklyn districts alone), so a cross-sectional correlation would be almost entirely a school-quality comparison.

WHAT THE SORTING DIAGNOSTICS ACTUALLY SHOW. The paper deserves credit for running Delhommer-style sorting tests and reporting that they fail. Tables 11a-d show that after adding school and cohort fixed effects, student race still strongly predicts same-race teacher share (Asian -0.1848***, Black -0.0277**, Latine -0.1626***, White +0.5951***), and for Asian and White students the magnitude GROWS when fixed effects are added, which by the paper's own stated criterion is direct evidence of within-school sorting. Tables 12a-d then show the sorting is on characteristics that independently predict the outcomes: Black students with an IEP have a higher Black-teacher share (+0.0076***) and Black students with lower 9-11 GPA have a higher Black-teacher share (-0.0007*** per GPA point, which over the 8.1-point GPA SD is a meaningful gradient); Asian and Latine ELL students have higher matched shares (+0.0159***, +0.0052***). This is exactly the omitted-variable structure that would generate a spurious negative for Black students and a spurious positive for Asian and Latine students in the GPA and attendance models. The honest reading of Tables 4-7 is therefore: these coefficients largely describe classroom assignment, not teacher influence. The authors reach a similar conclusion in the Discussion, which is to their credit, but the abstract does not.

THE TEXT-VERSUS-TABLE PROBLEM. This is the issue that should most change how a reader uses the paper, because it is not a matter of interpretation but of what the numbers say. Table 6 (matched teachers -> GPA) contains ten coefficients, all positive, all but one significant. The Black covariate-adjusted estimate is +5.1294 (SE 0.8581) and the unadjusted is +7.9322 (SE 1.0957). Yet the abstract announces 'a negative relationship for Black students,' the Results describe 'a 5.13-point decrease,' and roughly a page and a half of the Discussion is devoted to explaining that decrease (differential exposure, muted role-model effects, discipline disparities, a comparison-group composition argument). One of these is wrong, and the paper offers no internal check that would let a reader determine which. The same page also states that Table 6's no-covariate columns show 'no significant relationships,' when all five are starred, and misattributes the 4.6004 Asian coefficient (column 3, no covariates) to the covariate-adjusted specification. Table 5 (teachers of color -> attendance) is described as showing 'a negative and significant relationship ... for Black students' when the table's Black columns are +0.0108** and +0.0046 (ns) and the table contains no negative entries whatsoever. And the abstract's sorting claim - 'a negative relationship between the average number of days attended the prior year and the share of same-race teachers for both Black and Latine students' - is contradicted both by Table 12 (Black +0.0091 ns; Latine +0.0136**) and by the paper's own body text, which correctly calls this relationship positive. Any of these individually could be a proofreading slip; together they mean that specific numerical claims in this paper should be verified against the tables before being cited, and that the tables themselves cannot be assumed error-free.

MAGNITUDE INTERPRETATION. Even taking the tables at face value, the substantive story is far smaller than the prose implies. The regressor is a share, and the paper interprets its coefficients at a one-unit (0 to 1) change, which for most groups is many standard deviations outside the observed support. Table 1a gives the distributions: Asian students' matched share has SD 0.11 with a 25th-75th range of 0.04-0.18; Latine students' has SD 0.12 with a range of 0.06-0.20; Black students' has SD 0.20. Scaling the covariate-adjusted estimates to one SD gives: Asian attendance 0.0173 x 0.11 = 0.0019, i.e., about a fifth of a percentage point; Latine attendance 0.0107 x 0.12 = 0.0013; Asian GPA 2.9235 x 0.11 = 0.32 points on a 100-point scale, or about 0.04 SD of GPA; Latine GPA 3.6393 x 0.12 = 0.44 points, about 0.05 SD. The text's claim that the Asian attendance result 'implies an increase from 96% average attendance to 98%' describes a student who has an all-Asian teaching staff for four years - a case with essentially no support in the data, since the 75th percentile of Asian students' matched share is 0.18. The text further muddies this by describing a one-unit change as 'a change in the proportion ... of 1 percent,' which understates the scaling by a factor of 100. Readers should do the SD rescaling themselves for any number they quote.

BAD CONTROLS AND WHAT THEY DO TO THE BLACK-STUDENT ESTIMATE. The preferred college-enrollment specification includes grades 9-11 GPA and attendance as covariates. These are outcomes of the same treatment - the paper analyzes them as outcomes in Tables 4-7 - so including them in the enrollment model is a textbook bad-control problem. The authors gesture at this ('an overspecified model, which can lead to bias in our results that understate the findings') but the characterization is wrong: bad controls can bias in either direction, and the paper's own appendix shows the direction here is large. Table A4, which drops GPA and attendance, reports a Black-student coefficient of -0.0903*** (SE 0.0316); Table 8 column 6, which includes them, reports -0.0195 (SE 0.0296). So for Black students the choice of whether to condition on the mediators determines whether the paper reports a large, highly significant nine-percentage-point negative association or a precise null. For the pooled sample the choice is immaterial (Table A3: -0.0073 vs. -0.0023 vs. -0.0069), which is why the overall null is credible; for the subgroup that carries the paper's most-discussed finding, it is decisive and undiscussed.

The mobility argument in the Discussion inherits this problem. The claim that 'the results for Black students are driven by mobile students' rests on Table A5, which restricts to single-school students and reports -0.0142 (ns). But Table A5's covariate set includes 9-11 GPA and attendance while Table A4's does not, so the contrast changes two things at once. Against the correctly matched comparison - Table 8 column 6's -0.0195 on the full Black sample with the same covariates - restricting to single-school students changes essentially nothing. There is no mobility effect demonstrated here.

SELECTION INTO THE SAMPLE. The analytic sample requires four years of NYCPS course data, and the college models are run 'conditional on high school graduation.' Both conditions are plausibly affected by the treatment: Gershenson et al. (2022), which the paper cites approvingly in its opening paragraph, finds effects of same-race teachers on high school graduation itself. Conditioning on graduation is therefore conditioning on a post-treatment variable that is a collider between exposure and unobserved determinants of college-going, and the four-year requirement removes transfers, movers out of the district, and non-completers - precisely the margin where matching effects are most often found. Neither selection appears in the Limitations section, which instead focuses on the diffuseness of high school teacher influence, the college-for-all context, and between-school sorting. Readers should not extend the paper's nulls to any question about persistence, dropout, or graduation.

MEASUREMENT OF THE OUTCOMES. The college enrollment measure is under-specified in a way that matters. The Data section states that approximately 70% of NYCPS students had postsecondary records in the NSC data, while Table 3a reports an 83% enrollment rate for the analytic sample; the paper never reconciles these or says how students with no NSC match were coded. NSC coverage is also incomplete and non-uniform across institution types, with weaker coverage of for-profit and proprietary institutions - a gap that is correlated with student race and therefore differentially attenuates precisely the subgroup contrasts of interest. The Barron's selectivity analysis (Table 10) has a related problem: rankings exist for 118,289 of 184,287 enrollees, yet all six regressions report N = 201,370, meaning students at unranked institutions are apparently pooled with non-enrollees in the zero category of every model. The two significant coefficients there (-0.0119*** for 'less competitive,' -0.0074** for 'most competitive') are also an odd, non-monotone pair that no mechanism in the paper predicts, and Table 10 uniquely reports R2 rather than adjusted R2 and omits its cluster count.

SENSITIVITY ANALYSES. The Table A3/A4 robustness work is genuinely useful. The quantile-regression exercise is not. The paper estimates method-of-moments quantile regressions (Rios-Avila et al.) of college enrollment on match share and justifies the approach on the grounds that 'our outcome, college enrollment, is binary.' Quantile regression is not a fix for a binary outcome; the conditional quantiles of a Bernoulli variable take values in {0,1}, so Figure 1's uniformly insignificant quartile coefficients are a mechanical consequence of the outcome's support rather than evidence about heterogeneity. The parallel figures for GPA (B2) and attendance (B1) are legitimate applications of the method, and it is a shame the paper does not describe their results in the text.

INFERENCE AND MULTIPLICITY. Clustering at the school level with ~485 clusters is the right call and comfortably above the small-cluster threshold. What is missing is any accounting for the number of tests. Tables 4 through 9 report on the order of a hundred coefficients across five student groups, two predictors, three outcomes, and two specifications, and Table 10 adds six more. In the covariate-adjusted college-enrollment models - the paper's headline outcome - exactly one estimate clears p<0.05, and that one (Asian students, URM teacher share, +0.0604) is nonsignificant in its own no-covariate counterpart (+0.0264) and reverses the sign pattern of the other four groups. Under any correction it would not survive. Yet it is this single coefficient that the Policy section converts into a recommendation about recruiting Asian American teachers - a recommendation that additionally misreads the regressor, which by the paper's own Data section counts only Black, Latine, and Native teachers.

BOOKKEEPING. Several numbers do not reconcile, which is worth noting not as pedantry but because it affects whether a reader can reuse the paper's figures. The Data section says the final sample is 159,832 students; the tables report 202,655. Tables 1a and 1b report N = 153,081 with a note describing graduates of 2016-2018 and titles referencing 2016-2017 and 2018-2019; Table 3a's title says cohorts graduating between 2016 and 2018 - all of which conflict with the 2017-2020 window stated everywhere else. The text's own description of Table 3a is garbled in three places (Latine, White, and poverty shares). The reported 184,287 college enrollees exceeds 83% of 202,655. Table A1's adjusted R2 is printed as '0337' and Table A2's all-student SE as '(0.089)' where '(0.0089)' is almost certainly intended. Individually trivial; collectively they suggest the tables did not get a careful final pass, which is relevant given the sign problems above.

BOTTOM LINE FOR A READER. The design is well-suited to a descriptive question and the data are among the best available for this literature. One conclusion is firmly supported and should be taken seriously by the field: across four cohorts of NYC graduates, cumulative exposure to ethnoracially matched teachers over four years of high school shows no meaningful association with college enrollment, and this null is stable across every specification, covariate set, subsample, enrollment margin, and estimator the paper reports. That is a real and useful contribution, particularly as a counterweight to the strong causal findings from settings with random or quasi-random assignment. Everything else in the paper - the positive GPA and attendance patterns for Asian and Latine students, the disputed Black-student GPA result, the Asian college-enrollment result, and the selectivity findings - rests on within-school variation that the paper's own sorting diagnostics show is systematically related to student need, is reported at an unrealistic scale, and in several cases is described in the text in ways the tables do not support. Those results should be read as documenting how students are assigned to teachers in New York City, not as evidence about what matched teachers do for students.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's literature review is unusually interdisciplinary for this subfield, pulling together the economics of student-teacher match (Dee, Gershenson et al., Delhommer, Blazar), the psychology of role modeling (Morgenroth et al., Lockwood et al.), and the historical and qualitative scholarship on Black and Latine teachers (Givens, Brockenbrough, Fránquiz & Salinas, Kohli) into a mechanism-organized argument rather than a citation list. It also engages disconfirming evidence directly, which is rarer than it should be in this literature. But readers should note several verifiable citation problems and internal inconsistencies, a missing engagement with the field's main synthesis review and with the grading-bias literature that bears directly on the paper's GPA outcome, a college-access literature that is thin relative to the headline enrollment outcome, and a 'first study' novelty claim that is narrower than it sounds.

**Strengths:**

- Genuinely cross-disciplinary sourcing. Most papers in this space cite either the causal economics literature (Dee 2004; Gershenson, Hart, Lindsay & Papageorge 2022; Delhommer 2022; Fairlie, Hoffmann & Oreopoulos 2014) or the qualitative and historical scholarship on teachers of color (Givens 2021; Kohli 2018; Royal 2022; McKinney de Royston et al. 2021; Fránquiz & Salinas 2022), rarely both. This paper does both, and uses the qualitative work substantively rather than decoratively.
- The review is organized around three named mechanisms — role modeling, teacher expectations, and bias reduction — with each anchored to a distinct evidence base (Morgenroth et al. 2015 and Lockwood et al. 2004 for role modeling; Gershenson, Holt & Papageorge 2016 and Fox 2016 for expectations; Chin et al. 2020, Lindsay & Hart 2017 and Shirrell et al. for bias). This is a more useful architecture for a reader than a chronological survey, and it makes clear what each finding would and would not support.
- It engages evidence that cuts against its own framing. Jang (2020) is presented as a null in urban settings, Brockenbrough (2012) is used to complicate the role-model premise from the perspective of Black male teachers themselves, and Ladd & Sorensen (2017) is invoked to note that teacher experience and content difficulty also matter. The section explicitly stating that 'having a teacher of color is not a panacea for structural inequity' (citing Gist & Bristol 2022; Dixon et al. 2019; Kohli 2018) is a real corrective to how this literature is often summarized in policy settings.
- It correctly distinguishes two constructs that are frequently conflated — ethnoracial match specifically versus exposure to teachers of color generally — and traces each to its own antecedents (Dee 2004 and Lindsay & Hart 2017 for match; Blazar 2021, Cherng & Halpin 2016, Hess & Leal 1997 for teachers of color). Keeping these separate is one of the paper's more durable contributions to how readers should think about the evidence base.
- It brings Asian American students into a literature that overwhelmingly studies Black and, more recently, Hispanic students, and it correctly notes (via Rong et al. 2022) that teacher-diversity policy discourse tends to omit Asian American educators entirely.

**Weaknesses:**

- The field's main synthesis is absent. Redding's (2019) Review of Educational Research synthesis of the student-teacher racial/ethnic match literature — which concludes that measured effects on objective achievement are small and inconsistent, and that the more robust findings sit in teachers' subjective perceptions and evaluations of students — is not cited. Its omission matters directly: this paper's central positive findings are on GPA, which is a teacher-assigned, subjective measure.
- No engagement with the grading-bias / subjective-evaluation literature. Because GPA is assigned by the same teachers whose ethnoracial match is the predictor, a same-race GPA association can arise mechanically from differential grading rather than from any role-model, expectations, or bias-reduction channel. The review never raises this as an interpretation, and cites none of the work on race and subjective grading or on same-race teachers' course grades. Readers should treat the GPA results as ambiguous between 'students did better' and 'teachers graded differently.'
- The college-access literature is thin relative to the headline outcome. For a paper whose main dependent variable is college enrollment, the access literature is limited to Roderick, Nagaoka & Coca (2009), Perna (2015), Britton (2019), Britton & Spencer (2020), and Knight & Duncheon (2020). Missing entirely are the counselor literature (school counselors, not teachers, are the formal college-information channel in most U.S. high schools), the undermatch literature, and the application- and financial-aid-friction literature. This is consequential: the paper's null on enrollment is far less surprising once one knows that the field has located the enrollment bottleneck in counselors, aid paperwork, and institutional capacity rather than in classroom teachers.
- Several citations are internally inconsistent or unverifiable as given. In the introduction, Blazar (2021) is described as producing effects 'on the order of 0.45 standard deviations'; ten pages later the same study is described as 0.25 SD for engagement and happiness and roughly 0.25 SD for math and reading. Shirrell et al. is cited five times in text as 2023 but appears in the reference list only as Shirrell, Bristol & Britton (2024). Farmer-Hinton & Adams is cited in text as 2026 and listed as 2006. Roksa & Velez (2012) is cited in the introduction for the delayed-entry/completion claim but does not appear in the reference list at all. Yun & Kurlaender is cited as 2021 while the reference-list details (JESPAR 9(2), 143-168) correspond to a 2004 article.
- The 'first study' novelty claim is narrower than its phrasing. The paper asserts it is 'the first, to our knowledge, that examines student-teacher ethnoracial matching across all four years of high school,' and frames prior high school work as having 'focused mainly on matching in 11th and 12th grades.' Delhommer (2022) constructs cumulative course-level matches across Texas high schools, and Gottfried, Kirksey & Fletcher (2022) examine course-level match across high school (reporting the strongest results in grades 11-12, which is not the same as studying only those grades). What is actually distinctive here is the continuous four-year cumulative share within a single large urban district, not four-year coverage per se.
- Effect-size units in the secondary literature are reported ambiguously. Hess & Leal (1997) is summarized as '10% increase in the percentage of high school faculty... associated with a 3.6% increase in the likelihood of college enrollment' and Atkins et al. (2014) as '10% increase in the share of Black teachers... associated with a 9% increase in the share of Black students reporting a desire to graduate from college.' Percent versus percentage-point is never disambiguated, and neither antecedent's identification is characterized — Hess & Leal is a 1997 cross-sectional analysis of 62 districts with no within-school comparison, which is very weak by current standards but is presented alongside quasi-experimental work without that caveat.
- The 'urban districts are understudied' premise is thinly supported. The claim rests almost entirely on Jang (2020) for the proposition that match effects differ by urbanicity, and undersells a fair number of urban-district match studies — including the authors' own NYC discipline work and the Measures of Effective Teaching districts (one of which, as the paper itself notes, is New York City).
- The Asian American category is used without engaging the substantial literature on its heterogeneity. Given that NYC's Asian American student population spans groups with vastly different immigration histories, language backgrounds, and postsecondary trajectories, and given that this paper's clearest positive results and one of its policy recommendations are Asian-American-specific, the absence of any engagement with the disaggregation critique or the model-minority literature is a real gap.
- The review supplies no framework for interpreting the paper's own negative 'teachers of color' coefficients. Table 7 shows negative and significant associations between URM teacher share and GPA for every student group except White students. A literature review that had engaged teacher-experience and school-resource sorting (teachers of color in NYC are concentrated in lower-resource schools and are on average less experienced) would have equipped readers to read that pattern as a composition artifact. Ladd & Sorensen (2017) is cited once and never connected to it.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read this alongside Redding (2019, Review of Educational Research), 'A Teacher Like Me,' before treating the paper's GPA findings as evidence about student learning. Redding's synthesis of the match literature emphasizes that the most consistent match effects appear in teachers' subjective perceptions and evaluations, not in objective achievement — which is exactly the seam this paper's teacher-assigned-GPA outcome sits on.
- For the enrollment null, the essential companion literature is on school counselors and application frictions rather than on teachers. Before concluding that ethnoracial match 'does not matter' for college-going, read the work estimating individual counselor effects on postsecondary attainment and the FAFSA/application-assistance experiments. The paper's own theory of change routes college information through teachers (via Stanton-Salazar 1997), which is a defensible but incomplete account of how U.S. high schools actually distribute college knowledge.
- Treat the Blazar (2021) effect sizes in this paper as unreliable as reported: the introduction says 0.45 SD and the later discussion says 0.25 SD for the same study. Go to Blazar's own paper for the numbers before citing them, and note that the version cited here is an EdWorkingPaper preprint.
- Verify the Gershenson, Hart, Lindsay & Papageorge (2022) characterization before repeating it. The paper attributes a nine-percentage-point high school graduation increase and six-percentage-point college enrollment increase specifically to 'having a Black male teacher in grades 3-5' for Black boys. The STAR-based design assigns same-race (Black) teachers, with heterogeneity examined by student gender and family background; the 'male teacher' framing and these exact magnitudes should be checked against the AEJ:Policy article.
- Do not cite this paper as the first four-year high school match study without checking Delhommer (2022, Economics of Education Review) and Gottfried, Kirksey & Fletcher (2022, EEPA). The defensible novelty is the cumulative four-year exposure share estimated within schools in a single very large urban district — a narrower and more accurate way to describe what is new here.
- Track down the citations the reference list does not support: Roksa & Velez (2012), cited in the introduction, is missing from the reference list entirely; Shirrell et al. is cited throughout as 2023 but listed only as Shirrell, Bristol & Britton (2024, EEPA); Farmer-Hinton & Adams is 2026 in text and 2006 in the list; Yun & Kurlaender's year appears wrong. None of these are load-bearing for the results, but they mean the paper is not a reliable bibliographic waypoint for those specific works.
- Situate this paper as a descriptive urban-district companion to the causal match literature, not as an independent test of it. Its within-school associations are, by its own Tables 11 and 12, contaminated by systematic within-school sorting of students to teachers — Black students with IEPs and lower attendance are more likely to have Black teachers; Asian and Latine English learners are more likely to have same-race teachers. The mechanism framework in the literature review (role model / expectations / bias reduction) sets up hypotheses the design cannot adjudicate; the Discussion's suggestion that the attendance and GPA results provide 'suggestive evidence of the role model effect' should be read as speculation, not as a mechanism test.
- Read the Discussion's claim that these results 'were similar to those of Jang (2020)' with care. Jang's urban null is on ninth-grade math achievement; this paper finds positive within-school associations with attendance and GPA for Asian and Latine students and a null only on college enrollment. The alignment is overstated.
- Read this paper together with Shirrell, Bristol & Britton (2024, EEPA) on exclusionary discipline. Same three authors, same NYCPS administrative data, different outcome — the two are best understood as installments from one data agreement rather than as independent corroboration, and the discipline paper's design choices provide useful context for the choices made here.
- For the Asian American results specifically, supplement with the literature on disaggregating the pan-ethnic 'Asian American' category in education research. NYC's Asian American student population is highly heterogeneous, and the paper's positive Asian-student findings and its policy recommendation to recruit Asian American teachers are both pooled across groups with very different baseline postsecondary trajectories.
- Note the funding disclosure (Walton Family Foundation and Chan Zuckerberg Initiative) when reading the policy implications section, which recommends specific district recruitment and hiring interventions.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Coverage. The review is broad and, on the dimension of disciplinary range, genuinely strong. It moves from Dee (2004) and the STAR experiment through the quasi-experimental administrative-data generation (Egalite & Kisida 2018; Lindsay & Hart 2017; Gershenson, Hart, Lindsay & Papageorge 2022; Delhommer 2022; Gottfried, Kirksey & Fletcher 2022), to the random-assignment teachers-of-color evidence (Blazar 2021), to survey-based perception work (Cherng & Halpin 2016; Chin et al. 2020), to psychology (Morgenroth, Ryan & Peters 2015's motivational theory of role modeling; Lockwood et al. 2004; Allen & Collisson 2020), to sociology (Stanton-Salazar 1997 on institutional agents; Kalogrides, Loeb & Béteille 2013 on within-school class assignment; Hailey 2022 on racialized school preferences in NYC), to history (Givens 2021 on Black teaching under Jim Crow) and to qualitative work on teachers of color (Brockenbrough 2012; Kohli 2018; Royal 2022; McKinney de Royston et al. 2021; Fránquiz & Salinas 2022). Very few papers in this literature span that range. Readers who want a single orienting bibliography for the field could do worse than this reference list.

What is missing, and why it matters. The most consequential omission is the field's synthesis literature. Redding's (2019) RER review of student-teacher racial/ethnic match is not cited, nor is the book-length synthesis of teacher diversity research. This is not a completeness complaint — it changes how the paper's own results should be read. The synthesis literature's central methodological point is that match effects are most consistently detected in teachers' subjective judgments of students (perceptions, expectations, recommendations, referrals) and are smaller and less consistent on objective achievement. This paper's headline positive results are on GPA — a teacher-assigned, subjective measure — and on attendance, which is also recorded by teachers. The paper interprets the GPA association as evidence about student behavior and possible role-model effects. An equally consistent reading, and one the literature would have supplied had it been engaged, is differential grading: same-race teachers may assign systematically different grades to the same underlying performance. There is a real literature on race and subjective grading that speaks to exactly this, and none of it appears. A reader should hold the GPA finding as genuinely ambiguous between a student-behavior story and a teacher-evaluation story, and should notice that the paper does not offer them that ambiguity.

The second consequential gap concerns the outcome the title advertises. The paper's contribution is framed around postsecondary access, but the college-access literature it engages amounts to about half a dozen citations. Absent are the counselor literature (which is where the field has located much of the school-level variance in postsecondary enrollment), the undermatch literature (Bowen/Chingos/McPherson and successors), and the application- and aid-friction experiments. For a New York City study this is particularly costly: NYC's college-going landscape is dominated by CUNY, whose enrollment dynamics, direct-admission and application processes, and community-college capacity are the subject of their own substantial literature and of a body of NYC-specific research from local research organizations. None of that context appears. The practical effect is that the paper's null on enrollment is presented as a puzzle to be explained by teacher sorting and 'college for all' saturation, when the more parsimonious reading — one that the omitted literature would have supplied directly — is that the marginal high school teacher, matched or not, is simply not the binding constraint on whether a NYC graduate enrolls somewhere, and that the paper is underpowered to detect a channel that the field already expects to be small relative to counselors, aid, and institutional capacity.

Characterization accuracy. Most descriptions of prior work are broadly faithful, but several are worth verifying before repeating. The most concrete problem is internal: Blazar (2021) is described in the introduction as producing effects 'on the order of 0.45 standard deviations' on social-emotional, academic, and behavioral outcomes, and in the later 'Margin of Influence' section as producing 0.25 SD on engagement and happiness and approximately 0.25 SD on short-term math and reading. Two different magnitudes for the same study in the same paper; a reader cannot take either on faith. The Gershenson et al. (2022) summary attributes gains to 'having a Black male teacher in grades 3-5' — the STAR-based design turns on same-race assignment with heterogeneity by student gender and family background, so the 'male teacher' framing and the specific nine- and six-percentage-point figures should be checked at source. The Egalite & Kisida (2018) citation is asked to carry two claims, the second of which (that matched middle school students 'were more likely to report planning to attend college due to the influence of their teacher') is a stronger causal-attributional reading than a student-perception survey item typically supports. Hess & Leal (1997) and Atkins, Fertig & Wilkins (2014) are both reported with percent/percentage-point ambiguity and without any characterization of their identification; Hess & Leal in particular is a cross-sectional district-level association across 62 districts from 1992 survey data, and it is presented in the introduction as a substantive antecedent for the teachers-of-color-and-college-enrollment relationship without that caveat. Readers should not treat the 3.6% figure as comparable in evidentiary weight to the quasi-experimental estimates it sits beside.

There is also a cluster of bibliographic errors that are individually minor but collectively signal that the reference apparatus was not checked. Shirrell et al. is cited in text as 2023 on five occasions and appears in the reference list only as Shirrell, Bristol & Britton (2024, EEPA) — a reader searching for 'Shirrell et al. 2023' will find nothing. Farmer-Hinton & Adams is cited as 2026 in text and listed as 2006. Roksa & Velez (2012), which supports the introduction's claim that delayed college entry reduces degree completion, is not in the reference list at all. Yun & Kurlaender is dated 2021 in both places, but the volume, page, and DOI details correspond to a 2004 JESPAR article. Denessen et al. is dated 2020 against a Learning and Instruction volume that corresponds to a later year. None of these affect the analysis, but they mean the paper should not be used as a bibliographic waypoint for those particular works.

Novelty claims. Three are made, and each is somewhat oversold in its phrasing while being defensible in substance. First, 'the first, to our knowledge, that examines student-teacher ethnoracial matching across all four years of high school.' Delhommer (2022) builds cumulative course-level match measures across Texas high schools, and Gottfried et al. (2022) examine course-level match across high school grades. The paper's own framing — that prior high school work 'focused mainly on matching in 11th and 12th grades' — is asserted without citation support and does not accurately describe the two studies it names; Gottfried et al. report their strongest results in grades 11-12, which the paper appears to have converted into a claim about the scope of that study. What is actually new is the continuous cumulative four-year exposure share estimated with school fixed effects in a single very large urban district, and readers should cite it for that. Second, the urbanicity gap. The claim that few match studies examine urban districts leans on three citations and on Jang (2020) for the premise that effects differ by urbanicity; a fair amount of the modern match literature is in fact set in large urban districts, including the authors' own NYC work. Third, the match-versus-teachers-of-color distinction. This is the paper's most defensible novelty claim and, in my judgment, its most durable contribution to how the field should organize itself, even though the paper's own estimates on the teachers-of-color margin (uniformly negative for GPA in Table 7, across every student group but White students) look more like a school-composition and teacher-experience artifact than a substantive finding — a reading the review gives readers no tools to reach.

Engagement with conflicting evidence. Better than the field average, but selective. Jang (2020) and Brockenbrough (2012) are used well, and the paper deserves credit for building a whole subsection around the proposition that teachers of color are not a panacea. What is not engaged is the quantitative skepticism: the pattern of small and sometimes null effects across the match literature, the concern about which outcomes the effects show up in, and the confound between teacher race and teacher experience/school resources in districts where teachers of color are concentrated in the highest-need schools. The paper's Limitations section gestures at the last of these ('teachers of color are often working in schools with limited fiscal resources'), but the literature review never builds the case, so the Discussion has no framework to interpret its own most striking negative coefficients with. Similarly, the Discussion's assertion that these results 'were similar to those of Jang (2020)' overstates the alignment: Jang's urban null is on ninth-grade math achievement, whereas this paper finds positive within-school associations for attendance and GPA among Asian and Latine students and a null only on enrollment.

Placement in the field. Read this as a descriptive, within-school companion to the causal match literature — useful for what it documents about exposure patterns and sorting in the nation's largest district, and for extending attention to Asian American students whom most of this literature omits, but not as evidence about effects. The paper's own sorting diagnostics (Tables 11 and 12, following Delhommer's conventions) show substantial within-school sorting of students to same-race teachers on characteristics that independently predict the outcomes — Black students with IEPs and lower attendance toward Black teachers, Asian and Latine English learners toward same-race teachers. That is a finding in its own right and arguably the paper's most reliable one; it should discipline how readers interpret every coefficient in the paper, including the sign flips between Table 6 and Table 7. Finally, note that the paper is one of a series by these three authors on the same NYCPS data (the 2024 EEPA discipline paper being the closest sibling), and that it is funded by the Walton Family Foundation and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative — disclosed, and not disqualifying, but worth holding in mind when reading the policy recommendations about district hiring and recruitment.

A note on my own limits: I am reasonably confident about the structure of this literature and about the internal inconsistencies I have identified, which are verifiable within the document itself. I am working from memory on the exact magnitudes reported in Blazar (2021), Hess & Leal (1997), Atkins et al. (2014), and Gershenson et al. (2022), which is why I have framed those as items to verify rather than as errors. I am also less certain about the completeness of the NYC-specific college-access literature and about very recent work (2024-2026) in this subfield that may have appeared after the paper's literature search.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper is readable, conventionally organized, and unusually candid about its descriptive limits, but the exposition is not a reliable guide to its own evidence. Numbers quoted in the prose repeatedly disagree with the tables, the sample size stated in Methods matches no table in the paper, the abstract and introduction summarize findings that the corresponding tables do not show (and omit two significant findings that they do), and the introduction contradicts the results section on the direction of a key sorting result. A reader can trust the tables; they cannot safely quote the prose without re-deriving every number.

**Strengths:**

- Clear, conventional architecture (introduction, mechanism-organized literature review, single explicit research question, empirical approach, results, sensitivity, limitations, discussion, tiered implications) that makes the paper easy to navigate and easy to skim to the part a reader needs.
- The literature review is genuinely well organized: it is structured around three named candidate mechanisms (role model effects, expectations, bias reduction) plus a fourth framing section on 'ethnoracial matching vs. having a teacher of color', and it deliberately includes disconfirming evidence (Jang 2020; Brockenbrough 2012) rather than only supportive citations.
- Exemplary candor about causal status. The Empirical Models section explains at length why student fixed effects are infeasible in high school (tracking, multiple sections, course choice) and states plainly that 'This approach does not allow us to make plausibly causal claims'; the Limitations section repeats it. The paper does not oversell identification.
- Table notes are unusually informative for the field: they name the estimation command (reghdfe, mmqreg), state the clustering level, list every covariate explicitly, and note that adjusted R2 is reported. A reader can tell what was run from the exhibits alone.
- The sensitivity section is substantive rather than perfunctory: quantile regressions, models with and without the potentially mediating GPA/attendance controls, two Delhommer-style sorting tests, and a single-school-attenders subsample. The sorting tests (Tables 11a-d, 12a-d) are the most interesting material in the paper and are presented in enough detail to read on their own.

**Weaknesses:**

- The paper's headline claim about Black students appears to contradict its own Table 6. The text states that for Black students 'an increase in the proportion of Black teachers by 1 percent [is] associated with a 5.13-point decrease in GPA', and the abstract advertises 'a negative relationship for Black students'. Table 6 column 6 (Black, with covariates) is printed as 5.1294*** with no negative sign, and column 5 (Black, no covariates) as 7.9322*** -- the largest positive coefficients in the table. Minus signs are preserved elsewhere in the extracted text (Table 4 column 1 is -0.0051***; every cell of Table 7 is negative), so this is unlikely to be an extraction artifact. Either the table or the paper's central finding is wrong, and a reader cannot tell which.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The article itself settles which side is wrong: the table, not the prose. Table 12b (p. 17) reports the reverse regression of average GPA in grades 9–11 on Black-teacher share at −0.0041***, −0.0007*** and −0.0007***, negative in every column; Figure B1 (p. 26), drawn by the estimation software, plots the Table 4 (p. 10) column 2 coefficient at about −0.002 where the table prints +0.0020; and Table A4 (p. 25) prints −0.0903*** where Table 8 (p. 12) column 6 prints −0.0195. Two independent identities plus a demonstrated dropped sign elsewhere show that Table 6's Black-student columns lost their minus signs in typesetting, so the negative GPA relationship for Black students described in the abstract, results and discussion is the correct reading and the printed +5.13 is wrong. The attendance sub-claim is different: with covariates the Black-student estimate in Table 5 is 0.0046 (SE 0.0040), not significant under either sign, so "negative and significant" is unsupported whatever the sign. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages and replicated by an independent blind reader.

- Immediately above that, the text says 'We find no significant relationships between demographic matching and GPA in models without covariates (columns 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9).' Table 6 shows every one of those columns starred: 1.3368***, 4.6004***, 7.9322***, 5.5929***, 2.7692**. The sentence is flatly contradicted by the table it introduces.
- The Asian GPA magnitude is quoted from the wrong column. The text says 'When we include controls... For Asian students, our estimates suggest that increasing the share of demographically matched teachers by one unit is associated with a 4.6-point increase in GPA' -- but 4.6004 is column 3 (Asian, WITHOUT covariates); the with-covariates estimate is 2.9235. The Latine figure quoted in the same paragraph (3.64) does come from the with-covariates column, so the two are not comparable as presented.
- The Table 5 narration is also contradicted by the table. The text reports 'a negative and significant relationship between attendance rates and exposure to teachers of color for Black students', but Table 5 shows Black students at 0.0108** (no covariates) and 0.0046 (with covariates) -- both positive, and the covariate-adjusted estimate is not significant.
- The stated sample size matches nothing. Methods says 'Our final sample consisted of 159,832 students'; Table 3a reports N = 202,655; the regression tables report roughly 201,000-202,700; Tables 1a and 1b report N = 153,081.
