A separate figure, '184,287 students enrolled in college over the period of this study', is inconsistent with the reported 83% enrollment rate applied to 202,655 (which gives about 168,000).
- Tables 1a, 1b, and 3a are labeled with the wrong years. The sample is graduating cohorts 2017-2020 (as every regression table's note correctly states), but Table 1a is titled '2016-2017 and 2018-2019', Table 3a is titled 'for Cohorts Graduating Between 2016 and 2018', and the notes to 1a and 1b say 'We include all students who graduated from high school in the years 2016-2018.' Three different windows for one sample.
- The Table 3a narration garbles the comparison it is describing. The text says students with more than a quarter matched teachers 'were more likely to be Black (0.31 versus 0.26 for the full sample) or White (0.47 versus 0.16)... and were less likely to be Asian (0.06 vs 0.20) or Latine (0.36 versus 0.16)'. Table 3a gives Black .31/.25, White .51/.16, Asian .06/.20, and Latine .12/.37. The White and Latine figures are wrong, and the Latine pair as printed (0.36 versus 0.16) describes an increase while the sentence calls it a decrease. The poverty comparison is also off by a point in both cells (text 0.74 vs 0.83; table .75 vs .85).
- The introduction contradicts the results section on the direction of a sorting result. The intro says 'we find a negative relationship between the average number of days attended the prior year and the share of same-race teachers for both Black and Latine students.' The results section says the opposite: 'A positive relationship exists between the average number of days attended and the share of teachers of the same race for Asian and Latine students.' Table 12c (Latine) shows +0.0136**, i.e. positive; Table 12b (Black) shows +0.0091 with no stars, i.e. null. The Discussion then re-asserts the intro's version ('Black students with fewer days in school... were more likely to have a higher share of same-race teachers'), which Table 12b does not support.
- The abstract omits both statistically significant results outside the GPA/attendance story. It says 'the likelihood of student college enrollment was not related to the proportion of teachers of the same ethnoracial background nor the proportion of teachers of color' -- but Table 9 column 4 shows a significant positive effect for Asian students (0.0604**, roughly six percentage points), and that single coefficient is the basis for the paper's most concrete policy recommendation (recruiting Asian American teachers). The abstract also never mentions Table 7, where the share of Black/Latine/Native teachers is associated with GPA reductions of 2.8 to 4.3 points for every student group except White (all p<0.01). That result gets one sentence in Results and is never discussed.
- 'Teachers of color' means two different things. The paper defines teachers of color as 'Asian American, Black, Latine, or Native American' and then says 'we carried out our analyses using only Black, Latine, or Native teachers.' Tables 5, 7, and 9 accordingly label the predictor 'URM teachers', but the abstract, results prose, and discussion all call it 'teachers of color'. The consequence is easy to miss: for Asian students, the 'teachers of color' variable excludes their own matched group entirely, so Tables 5/7/9 for Asian students are not measuring what the prose says.
- The table notes contradict the tables' own Control Variables row. Every regression note says 'the third and fourth columns are Asian students with and without covariates' (and likewise for 5/6, 7/8, 9/10) after describing columns 1 and 2 as 'without' then 'with'. The Control Variables row reads N, Y, N, Y..., so the order is without-then-with throughout. Since the text quotes results by column number, this note error compounds the sign and magnitude errors above.
- Appendix A4 quietly overturns a main-text claim. The sensitivity text says the point estimates 'are relatively similar for models that include GPA and number of days present... and models that exclude both variables', citing Tables A3 and A4. But Table A3 reports only the pooled sample. Table A4 (no GPA/attendance controls, by race) shows Black students at -0.0903*** -- a large, highly significant negative college-enrollment coefficient -- against -0.0195 (n.s.) in the main Table 8. The sentence 'relatively similar' is doing a lot of work.
- The single-school robustness check is framed against a result the main specification does not contain. Both the sensitivity text ('the negative relationship... is no longer significant') and the Discussion ('We find that the results for Black students are driven by mobile students') presuppose a significant negative Black coefficient in Table 8. Table 8 column 6, the covariate-adjusted Black model, is -0.0195 with no stars; the significant -0.1459*** is column 5, the model with no covariates.
- Throughout, coefficients on a 0-1 share are narrated inconsistently as 'a 1 unit increase' and 'a change... of 1 percent'. Both appear in the same paragraph for the same table (Asian, 'by one unit'; Latine, 'of 1 percent'; Black, 'by 1 percent'). Only the first is right; the others are off by a factor of 100. Separately, every headline magnitude is a full 0-to-100% extrapolation ('an increase from 96% average attendance to 98%') far outside the observed range -- Asian students average 13% matched teachers and Latine students 14% (Table 1a).
- The method is called 'quartile regression' throughout (six times, plus in three figure notes), though the estimator is method-of-moments quantile regression -- endnote 3 correctly says 'the mmqreg command in Stata for each quantile'. The Figure 1 discussion also gives a non-sequitur reason for a null: 'as seen by the confidence intervals that include zero, and the negative coefficients.'
- Smaller consistency problems accumulate: the Limitations section opens 'this is descriptive and not casual work'; Table 2b reports 36,158 teachers while Table 2a's license totals are 28,612 ('79.22%') with no explanation of the missing fifth; Table 3a's four-year (.60) plus two-year (.26) exceeds total college enrollment (.83) with no note explaining the overlap; Table 3a's note describes variables ('average number of days attended') that are not in the table; students with IEPs are called 'students with learning differences' (Table 3a), 'students with disabilities' (table notes), and 'students with IEP' (Table 12) in three places; Table 12's panels are printed out of order (12a, 12b, 12d, 12c); Tables A4 and A5 carry identical titles even though A5 is the single-school subsample; and there are stray typos in table cells (Table 5 column header '(1`0)', Table 7 headers '(1)(2)(2)(4)', Table 9 N '31,9935', Table 11c R2 '0.31`', Table A1 Adj. R2 '0337').

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not quote a number from this paper's prose. Every headline magnitude in the Results section either comes from the wrong column, carries the wrong sign, or uses the wrong units. Read the tables directly and re-derive anything you plan to cite.
- Treat Table 6 as the paper's central puzzle, not its central finding. The 'negative relationship between same-race teachers and GPA for Black students' -- which is in the abstract, the introduction, the Results section, and two full paragraphs of the Discussion -- corresponds to a cell printed as 5.1294***, positive. Check the published PDF yourself before citing this paper for a negative Black-student GPA association; if the table is correct, the paper's most-quotable claim is the reverse of its evidence.
- Read the abstract as incomplete rather than as a summary. It omits the one significant college-enrollment result in the paper (Asian students, teachers of color, Table 9 column 4, +0.0604**), which is what the Policy section actually recommends acting on; and it omits the large negative association between URM-teacher share and GPA for all non-White groups (Table 7). Anyone stopping at the abstract will leave with a materially different picture than the tables give.
- Whenever the paper says 'teachers of color', substitute 'Black, Latine, or Native teachers' and re-read the sentence. The measure excludes Asian American teachers by construction, so Tables 5, 7, and 9 for Asian students describe exposure to teachers who are, by definition, not ethnoracially matched to them.
- Read the odd/even column structure of Tables 4-9 for yourself. The notes say 'with and without covariates' but the Control Variables row says N then Y; the covariate-adjusted estimate is always the even column. Several of the paper's claims are true of one column and false of the other, and the text does not consistently say which it means.
- The most trustworthy and most interesting part of the paper is the sorting evidence, Tables 11a-d and 12a-d. Those tables are internally consistent, the results section narrates them correctly (unlike the introduction and discussion, which reverse the attendance result), and they document substantial within-school sorting of students to same-race teachers. If you read only one section, read this one -- it is also the strongest argument for treating every other result in the paper as confounded.
- Check Appendix Table A4 before accepting the claim that dropping GPA and attendance controls leaves estimates 'relatively similar'. For Black students the college-enrollment coefficient moves from -0.0195 (n.s., Table 8) to -0.0903*** (Table A4). The pooled Table A3 is stable; the by-race results are not.
- Ignore the sample size given in Methods (159,832). The analytic sample in every regression is approximately 201,000-202,700, and the descriptive Tables 1a/1b use 153,081. Similarly ignore the year ranges in the titles and notes of Tables 1a, 1b, and 3a (variously 2016-2017/2018-2019 and 2016-2018); the cohorts are 2017-2020 graduates, as stated in the regression table notes.
- The Literature Review and Implications sections can be skimmed; neither carries evidence. The Empirical Approach section's discussion of why student fixed effects fail in high school (about one page) is the load-bearing methodological argument and should not be skipped -- it is where the paper honestly bounds what it can claim.
- Remember the sample is conditional on high school graduation and on having four years of NYCPS course data. Despite the title's 'Postsecondary Access', the paper cannot speak to matching effects that operate through dropout, and the 83% baseline college-enrollment rate reflects that selection. NSC coverage is also only about 70% of NYCPS students, and Barron's rankings cover only 64% of the enrollees in Table 10.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a well-structured paper whose prose has come apart from its exhibits. The organization itself is fine and in places better than fine: a single explicitly numbered research question, a literature review built around three named mechanisms that the Discussion later returns to one by one, an Empirical Approach section that argues carefully for why a weaker design (school and cohort fixed effects) was chosen over a stronger one (student fixed effects), and an honest limitations section. Table notes name the Stata commands and enumerate the covariates. A reader looking for the shape of the argument will find it easily. The problem is fidelity, and it is pervasive enough to change how the paper should be used.

The most serious issue sits at the center of the paper. The Results section states: 'For Black students, our models with covariates show a negative and significant relationship between the share of demographically matched teachers and GPA, with an increase in the proportion of Black teachers by 1 percent associated with a 5.13-point decrease in GPA.' Table 6, column 6 (Black, with covariates) is printed as 5.1294*** with no negative sign; column 5 (Black, without covariates) is 7.9322***. Every cell in Table 6 is positive, and the Black cells are the largest positives in the table. This is not obviously an extraction artifact: minus signs survive elsewhere in the same document (Table 4 column 1 is -0.0051***, Table 8 column 5 is -0.1459***, and all ten cells of Table 7 are negative). The claim propagates -- into the abstract ('a negative relationship for Black students'), into the introduction, and into two full Discussion paragraphs that theorize about why matching might not help Black students. If Table 6 is right, the paper's most citable finding is the sign-flip of its own evidence; if the text is right, the printed table is wrong. Either way a reader cannot resolve it from the article and should verify against the published PDF before citing.

The same paragraph contains two further errors. It opens 'We find no significant relationships between demographic matching and GPA in models without covariates (columns 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9)' -- all five of those columns are starred in Table 6 (1.3368***, 4.6004***, 7.9322***, 5.5929***, 2.7692**). And the Asian magnitude is taken from the uncontrolled column: the text introduces the sentence with 'When we include controls, however...' and then reports 4.6, which is column 3 (no covariates); the with-covariates estimate is 2.9235. The Latine figure in the same sentence (3.64) is correctly from the with-covariates column, so the two race groups are being compared across different specifications without the reader being told.

Table 5 is narrated the same way. The text claims 'a negative and significant relationship between attendance rates and exposure to teachers of color for Black students'; the table shows 0.0108** without covariates and 0.0046 (unstarred) with them -- positive and null, respectively.

Sample-size reporting is a second cluster of trouble. Methods states 'Our final sample consisted of 159,832 students, with one observation per student.' No table in the paper reports that number. Table 3a and the sorting tables report N = 202,655; the outcome regressions report 201,000-202,700; Tables 1a and 1b report 153,081. In the selectivity subsection the paper says 'of the 184,287 students enrolled in college over the period of this study' -- but 83% of 202,655 is about 168,000, so that figure does not follow from the paper's own descriptives either. Compounding this, the descriptive tables carry three different year windows for one sample: Table 1a's title says '2016-2017 and 2018-2019', its note says 'graduated from high school in the years 2016-2018', Table 3a's title says 'Cohorts Graduating Between 2016 and 2018', while every regression note and the abstract say 2017-2020.

The Table 3a narration in the text does not survive checking either. The text reports the matched-versus-full-sample comparison as Black '0.31 versus 0.26', White '0.47 versus 0.16', Asian '0.06 vs 0.20', Latine '0.36 versus 0.16', poverty '0.74 versus 0.83'. Table 3a gives .31/.25, .51/.16, .06/.20, .12/.37, and .75/.85. Only the Asian pair is right. Worse, the Latine pair is embedded in a clause saying these students were 'less likely to be... Latine (0.36 versus 0.16)', which as printed reads as an increase.

A third cluster involves the sorting analysis, which is otherwise the paper's best evidence. The Results section reads Table 12 correctly: 'A positive relationship exists between the average number of days attended and the share of teachers of the same race for Asian and Latine students' (Table 12a: 0.0661**; Table 12c: 0.0136**). But the Introduction's summary of findings says the opposite -- 'a negative relationship between the average number of days attended the prior year and the share of same-race teachers for both Black and Latine students' -- and the Discussion repeats the introduction's version: 'Black students with fewer days in school and with disabilities were more likely to have a higher share of same-race teachers' and 'Black students who had lower rates of attendance... were more likely to have a higher share of Black teachers.' Table 12b's attendance coefficients for Black students are 0.0418, 0.0020, and 0.0091, none starred. The IEP half of that sentence is correct (0.0076***); the attendance half is not supported anywhere in the paper.

Abstract fidelity is a specific concern because two significant results are missing from it. First, Table 9 column 4 shows a significant positive relationship between URM-teacher share and college enrollment for Asian students (0.0604**), described in the text as 'a six-percentage point increase' and used in the Policy section to argue that 'future policy efforts should also center on recruitment initiatives aimed at Asian American teachers.' The abstract says only that college enrollment 'was not related to' either predictor. Second, and larger, Table 7 shows the share of Black/Latine/Native teachers associated with GPA declines of -3.27 (all), -4.25 (Asian), -2.80 (Black), and -3.11 (Latine), all at p<0.01. That result gets exactly one sentence in the Results section and no mention at all in the abstract, the introduction's findings summary, or the Discussion. Readers relying on the abstract will not know the paper contains it.

A terminology trap runs through the whole paper. 'Teachers of color' is defined as 'Asian American, Black, Latine, or Native American' but operationalized, as Methods states in a single clause, 'using only Black, Latine, or Native teachers.' The tables honor this by labeling the predictor 'URM teachers'; the abstract, Results prose, Discussion, and Implications all revert to 'teachers of color.' For Asian American students -- the group with the paper's only significant college-enrollment result -- this means the 'teachers of color' variable excludes their own matched group by construction, an interpretive point the paper never surfaces.

Two presentational issues make the text-table checking harder than it should be. First, every regression note describes the column layout as 'the third and fourth columns are Asian students with and without covariates' (and so on for each pair) immediately after correctly describing columns 1 and 2 as without-then-with; the Control Variables row (N, Y, N, Y...) confirms without-then-with throughout. Since so many of the paper's claims hold in one column and not the other, this note error is not cosmetic. Second, coefficients on a 0-1 share are described inconsistently as 'a 1 unit increase' and 'a change... of 1 percent' within a single paragraph, and every reported magnitude is a full 0-to-100% extrapolation ('an increase from 96% average attendance to 98% average attendance for Asian American students') well outside the support of the data, where Asian students average 13% matched teachers.

Finally, two robustness claims should be checked rather than taken on faith. The sensitivity text says estimates are 'relatively similar' with and without the GPA/attendance controls, citing Tables A3 and A4; A3 covers only the pooled sample and is indeed stable, but A4 shows the Black coefficient at -0.0903*** against -0.0195 (n.s.) in Table 8. And both the sensitivity section and the Discussion ('We find that the results for Black students are driven by mobile students') frame the single-school check as overturning a negative Black result that the paper's preferred specification, Table 8 column 6, does not contain -- the significant -0.1459*** is the model with no covariates at all.

Minor but accumulating: the estimator is called 'quartile regression' six times in text and in all three figure notes, though endnote 3 and the mmqreg command indicate quantile regression; the Limitations section opens 'this is descriptive and not casual work'; Table 3a's four-year (.60) and two-year (.26) shares sum above its own college-enrollment share (.83) with no note explaining the overlap; Table 2b reports 36,158 teachers while Table 2a's license totals reach only 28,612 ('79.22%'), unexplained; the IEP variable is named three different ways across exhibits; Table 12's panels print in the order a, b, d, c; Tables A4 and A5 share a title despite different samples; and several table cells carry stray characters ('(1`0)', '31,9935', '0.31`', '0337', duplicate column header '(2)' in Table 7).

On balance the writing is clear at the sentence level and the architecture is sound, but the exposition cannot be relied on as a description of the results. Given the volume of text-table disagreement -- including on the finding the abstract leads with -- 'weak' is the right calibration for a published article: readers should use the tables and treat the narrative as a hypothesis about what the tables say.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This paper contributes a large, well-powered descriptive null: in the nation's largest urban district, cumulative exposure to ethnoracially matched teachers across all four high school years is not associated with college enrollment, conditional on graduating. That null — and the sorting diagnostics that accompany it — is the paper's real and citable contribution, and it is a useful counterweight to a literature dominated by positive findings. The paper's more quotable claims (the four-year-exposure novelty framing, and especially the 'negative relationship for Black students') are considerably weaker than the null, and one of them appears to contradict the paper's own tables.

**Strengths:**

- A genuine, well-powered descriptive null on a question the field cares about: with ~200,000 students across four graduating cohorts (2017-2020) in NYC Public Schools linked to National Student Clearinghouse records, the estimates for college enrollment are precise enough that the null is informative rather than merely underpowered. The all-student point estimate with covariates is -0.0073 (SE 0.0068), and group-specific estimates are similarly small and insignificant. Nulls at this scale are hard to publish and worth having in the record.
- The construct is new in a defensible way. Prior work largely measures whether a student had one matched teacher, or match in a single grade (Delhommer 2022 in 9th grade; most others in 11th-12th). Measuring the cumulative *share* of matched teachers across all four high school years — an average of 27 teachers per student — is a different and arguably more policy-relevant dose measure, and the paper is correct that no prior study has done this across all four years.
- The paired same-race-match vs. teacher-of-color contrast is a real conceptual contribution. Most of the literature treats these as interchangeable; the paper runs both on the same sample and finds they do not move together (e.g., teachers-of-color share is positively associated with college enrollment for Asian students, B = 0.0604, p < 0.05, where same-race share is not). That divergence is itself an interesting finding the field should absorb.
- The sorting diagnostics (Tables 11a-d, 12a-d) are more valuable than the headline regressions. Following Delhommer (2022), the paper shows that student race predicts same-race teacher share *more* strongly once school fixed effects are added (White students: 0.5659 to 0.5951; Asian: -0.1494 to -0.1848), and that within-race characteristics predict match (Black students with IEPs and lower attendance get more Black teachers; Asian and Latine ELL students get more matched teachers). This is a documented, quantified obstacle to identification in high-school matching work generally, and is useful to anyone designing a future study in this setting.
- The paper is honest about being descriptive. It says so in the abstract framing, in the Empirical Approach ('This approach does not allow us to make plausibly causal claims'), and again in Limitations, and it explains why the student-fixed-effects strategy used in elementary settings breaks down in high school (tracking, course choice, multiple sections). That candor is what keeps the contribution usable rather than misleading.
- The setting genuinely matters. NYC has the demographic mismatch (85%+ students of color vs. 42% teachers of color) and the college-enrollment gaps the literature invokes as motivation, and prior matching evidence in urban districts is thin and mixed (Jang 2020 found urban nulls). Testing whether the matching result replicates in the paradigm case for the policy is worth doing.

**Weaknesses:**

- The paper's most quotable claim — the abstract's 'negative relationship for Black students' — is contradicted by the corresponding table as published. Table 6 (same-race share on GPA) reports 7.9322*** without covariates and 5.1294*** (SE 0.8581) with covariates for Black students, both positive; the text describes this same coefficient as 'a 5.13-point decrease in GPA.' The same reversal appears for attendance: Table 5 shows Black-student coefficients on teacher-of-color share of 0.0108** and 0.0046, both positive, while the text reports 'a negative and significant relationship.' Minus signs survive the PDF elsewhere in the same tables (Table 4 column 1 is -0.0051***; all of Table 7 is negative), so this is not obviously an extraction artifact. Until resolved, the paper's signature finding cannot be relied upon in either direction.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: the article's own appendix settles the sign.*

- The negative college-enrollment result for Black students is entirely a specification artifact and the paper does not say so plainly. The Black-student coefficient moves from -0.1459*** (no covariates, Table 8 col. 5), to -0.0903*** (covariates without GPA/attendance, Table A4), to -0.0195 and insignificant (with lagged GPA and attendance, Table 8 col. 6), to insignificant again when restricted to single-school students (Table A5). The paper flags the overspecification concern in one sentence, then attributes the pattern to 'mobile students' in the Discussion. A reader cannot tell from the paper whether the null or the negative is the better summary, because the controls doing the work (GPA, attendance) are plausibly mediators of the very mechanism under study.
- The novelty claim is narrower than the framing implies. 'First study across all four high school years' is a claim about a measurement window, not about identification, data access, or a new question. Delhommer (2022) already estimated matching effects on high school graduation and college enrollment on Texas administrative data with a stronger design; Gershenson et al. (2022) has experimental variation from STAR. On the outcome named in the title — postsecondary access — this paper's design is weaker than the two studies it positions itself against, so its four-year exposure measure buys breadth at the cost of credibility.
- The null is not cleanly interpretable as evidence against a matching effect, because the paper's own diagnostics show the treatment variable is systematically assigned. If Black students with IEPs and low attendance are sorted toward Black teachers within schools, and Asian/Latine ELL students toward matched teachers, then the estimated associations blend any teacher effect with the selection process — and the direction of that bias differs by group. The paper acknowledges this in the Discussion but still writes the abstract and implications as if the associations were informative about teachers.
- Sample reporting is internally inconsistent enough to complicate citation. The text states a final sample of 159,832 students; the regression tables report N up to 202,655; Table 1a/1b report N = 153,081; and the notes to Tables 1a, 1b, and 3a describe 'students who graduated between 2016 and 2018' while the data section and every regression note specify 2017-2020 cohorts. A reader quoting a sample size or cohort window from this paper should not assume any one figure is the right one.
- The mechanism discussion outruns the evidence. The paper offers the GPA/attendance results as 'suggestive evidence of the role model effect' and then, for Black students, proposes a compositional story (that low-share Black students are a different type of student) that it does not test — while the sorting tables actually point toward a different and more mundane explanation, that matched teachers are assigned to higher-need students. The paper does not adjudicate between them.
- Restricting the sample to students with four full years of NYCPS course data conditions on high school persistence, and all college-enrollment models condition on graduation. Both are selections on outcomes plausibly affected by teacher exposure. The paper does not discuss this, and it means the results speak only to students who were already on the persistence-and-graduation path.
- NSC coverage is reported at roughly 70% of NYCPS students, and Barron's selectivity ratings are available for only ~64% of enrollees. Neither the enrollment measurement error nor the selectivity-analysis attrition is characterized by student race, even though differential coverage by institution type (proprietary, community, special-mission colleges) would fall unevenly across the very groups being compared.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the descriptive finding that, in a very large urban district, cumulative exposure to ethnoracially matched high school teachers is not associated with college enrollment conditional on graduation. This is the paper's best-supported claim, it is precisely estimated, and it is a legitimate counterweight to the mostly-positive matching literature.
- CITE IT FOR: the documented extent of within-school sorting of students to same-race teachers in a large urban high school system (Tables 11 and 12) — specifically that student race predicts matched-teacher share more strongly *after* adding school fixed effects, and that IEP status, ELL status, and prior attendance predict match within race. This is a methodological warning that should be cited by anyone planning a high-school matching study.
- CITE IT FOR: descriptive exposure statistics in NYC — Black students average 24% Black teachers and 35% teachers of color; Latine students 14% Latine teachers; Asian students 13% Asian teachers; White students 75% White teachers despite being the smallest student group. These are useful, citable facts about the mismatch in the nation's largest district.
- CITE IT FOR: the observation that same-race match and teacher-of-color exposure behave differently as predictors and should not be treated as substitutes in this literature.
- DO NOT LEAN ON: the claim that same-race teachers are negatively associated with outcomes for Black students. The GPA and attendance coefficients in Tables 5 and 6 are positive as printed while the text calls them negative, and the negative college-enrollment estimate disappears once GPA/attendance controls or a single-school restriction are applied. Citing this as a finding is not currently defensible.
- DO NOT LEAN ON: the null as evidence that student-teacher matching does not affect college-going. The design is associational, the treatment is demonstrably non-randomly assigned (by the paper's own diagnostics), and the college-enrollment models control for GPA and attendance — the most likely mediators of any matching effect. The correct summary is 'no association in this descriptive within-school comparison,' not 'no effect.'
- DO NOT LEAN ON: the positive GPA and attendance results for Asian and Latine students as causal or as role-model evidence. They appear only in covariate-adjusted specifications (GPA effects are null without covariates in Table 6, columns 1, 3, 5, 7, 9), and the same sorting that the paper documents could generate them.
- DO NOT LEAN ON: the college-selectivity results (Table 10). Barron's ratings cover only ~64% of enrollees, the coefficients are small and inconsistently signed across categories, and each is a separate linear probability model against all other categories.
- DO NOT LEAN ON: any single sample size or cohort window quoted from the paper; the text (159,832), the tables (up to 202,655), and Table 1 (153,081) disagree, as do the 2017-2020 and 2016-2018 cohort descriptions.
- OPEN QUESTION a reader should know remains unresolved: whether the divergence between short-run outcomes (GPA, attendance) and college enrollment reflects a real mediation failure — teachers move grades but grades do not convert to enrollment for these students — or is an artifact of controlling for the mediator. Nothing in this paper settles it.
- OPEN QUESTION: whether cumulative share across four years is the right dose measure at all. The paper's own limitation — a student may have 8 teachers a year for 40 minutes each — suggests that which subject, which grade, and which course level the match occurs in may matter more than the average. The authors say they are pursuing this in follow-on work.
- GENERALIZATION BOUNDARY: NYC is not a typical district. It is choice-rich, heavily segregated by parental choice (the paper cites Hailey 2022), has an unusually large Asian American student population, has a 'college for all' district posture, and has an 83% baseline college enrollment rate among graduates. A null here does not license a null elsewhere, and the paper is reasonably careful about this in Limitations even as the title is not.
- STANDING IN THE LITERATURE: this is now the best available *descriptive* evidence on four-year cumulative high school matching exposure in a large urban district, but it does not displace Delhommer (2022) or Gershenson et al. (2022) as the best evidence on whether matching affects postsecondary outcomes. Position it as scope-and-setting evidence alongside Jang (2020)'s urban nulls, not as a competing estimate.

**Detailed Commentary:**

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW

Strip away the framing and three things here are new. First, the exposure measure: the share of a student's teachers across all four high school years who share their ethnoracial identity, built from student-course-year records over an average of 27 teachers per student. Prior high school work has measured match in a single grade (Delhommer 2022 in ninth; most others in eleventh and twelfth) or as a binary 'had at least one.' Second, the setting-plus-outcome combination: NYCPS administrative records linked to National Student Clearinghouse enrollment for four graduating cohorts, in the district that is the paradigm case for the teacher-diversity policy argument. Third, and least noticed in the paper's own framing, the head-to-head of same-race match against teacher-of-color exposure on identical samples and specifications.

What is not new is the question, and what is weaker than prior work is the design. The paper positions itself against Gershenson et al. (2022), which has experimental variation from Project STAR, and Delhommer (2022), which has Texas administrative data and a stronger identification strategy. Both already estimated matching effects on college enrollment. This paper's response is breadth of exposure measurement, not credibility of identification — school and cohort fixed effects with student covariates, explicitly labeled descriptive. That is an honest trade, but readers should understand it as adding a differently-measured association in a new setting, not as improving on prior estimates.

WHAT THE FINDINGS ACTUALLY SUPPORT

The most defensible contribution is the college-enrollment null, and it is a real one. With roughly 200,000 students, the all-student estimate of -0.0073 (SE 0.0068) rules out anything but small effects of moving from no matched teachers to all matched teachers — a dose swing far larger than any realistic policy could produce. Group-specific estimates for Asian (-0.0069), Black (-0.0195), Latine (-0.0523), and White (-0.0279) students are similarly indistinguishable from zero. Nulls at this precision are worth publishing and worth citing, particularly because the matching literature has a visible positive-results tilt and because the outcome is one the field routinely invokes when arguing for teacher-diversity policy.

But the null carries an important qualifier that the paper states once and then largely sets aside: the preferred college-enrollment specification controls for GPA and attendance in grades 9-11. If matched teachers work through grades and attendance — which is precisely the mechanism the paper's own GPA and attendance analyses are set up to test — then conditioning on them removes the pathway before measuring the outcome. Table A3 partially addresses this (the all-student estimate is -0.0023 without GPA and attendance, still null), so the aggregate null survives. The subgroup story does not: Table A4 shows a Black-student coefficient of -0.0903*** without those controls, against -0.0195 and insignificant with them. Whether the honest summary for Black students is 'no association' or 'a substantial negative association that vanishes when you condition on mediators' depends on a modeling choice the paper does not resolve.

THE GAP BETWEEN THE QUOTABLE CLAIM AND THE SUPPORTED ONE

This paper has an unusually sharp version of the quotable-versus-supported problem, and readers should be warned about it specifically. The abstract's distinguishing claim is 'a positive relationship between the share of ethnoracially matched teachers and student attendance rate and GPA for Asian and Latine students and a negative relationship for Black students.' That contrast is what will get cited; it is provocative, it complicates a comfortable narrative, and the Discussion builds a substantial theoretical apparatus around it (compositional differences among Black students, muted role-model effects, disparate discipline as a competing in-school force).

The tables do not support it as printed. In Table 6, the Black-student coefficient on same-race teacher share predicting GPA is 5.1294*** (SE 0.8581) with covariates and 7.9322*** without — the largest positive coefficients in the table, larger than those for Asian (2.9235***) or Latine (3.6393***) students. The text describes this identical coefficient as 'a 5.13-point decrease in GPA.' In Table 5, teacher-of-color share predicting attendance for Black students is 0.0108** and 0.0046 — positive — while the text reports 'a negative and significant relationship between attendance rates and exposure to teachers of color for Black students.' Negative signs are clearly preserved elsewhere in the same document (Table 4 column 1 shows -0.0051***; every coefficient in Table 7 is negative; Table 8 column 5 shows -0.1459***), so this does not read as a rendering failure.

This matters for use, not for blame. Whether the error is in the tables or in the text, a reader cannot presently determine the sign of the paper's headline subgroup finding, and should therefore not cite it. That the paper then constructs several paragraphs of mechanism theorizing on top of the disputed sign compounds the problem: the theoretical discussion of why Black students might show a negative association would need to be rewritten entirely if the tables are the correct version.

SORTING: THE UNDERAPPRECIATED CONTRIBUTION

The sorting analyses are, in my judgment, the most durable thing in the paper, and they are presented as a sensitivity check rather than a finding. Following Delhommer's diagnostic, the paper shows that adding school fixed effects makes the race-to-match relationship stronger, not weaker, for Asian (-0.1494 to -0.1848), Black (-0.0167 to -0.0277**), and White (0.5659 to 0.5951***) students. That is direct evidence of within-school sorting, which is exactly the confound that school fixed effects were supposed to address. Table 12 then shows the sorting is on characteristics that predict the outcomes: Black students with IEPs and lower prior attendance get more Black teachers; Asian and Latine ELL students get more matched teachers; White students who changed schools or are ELL get fewer White teachers.

The implication is that within-school comparisons of matched-teacher exposure in high school are comparing systematically different students, in group-specific directions. Anyone planning future work in this setting should cite these tables, and anyone citing this paper's associations should cite them too, as the reason those associations are not interpretable as teacher effects. It also suggests that the paper's own mechanism story runs the wrong way: the Discussion reaches for role-model theory when its diagnostics point toward assignment of high-need students to matched teachers, an explanation that would generate a spurious negative association for Black students without any teacher effect at all.

GENERALIZABILITY AND BOUNDARIES

The Limitations section is honest about the descriptive design, the difficulty of attributing influence when a student has eight teachers for forty minutes each, the 'college for all' district context, and non-random sorting into schools. What it does not draw boundaries around is how atypical NYC is on the dimensions that matter for this question. Baseline college enrollment among graduates is 83%, which is high and compresses the outcome; the district's Asian American student population (16.5%) is far larger than in most districts, and the Asian-student results drive several of the paper's positive findings; parental school choice produces heavy ethnoracial sorting across schools (the paper cites Hailey 2022 on this) which means the within-school comparison set differs substantially by group. A null in this environment travels less far than the title's unqualified 'Evidence From New York City' suggests.

The conditioning is also worth naming. The sample requires four years of NYCPS course data, and college-enrollment models are conditional on graduation. Both are selections on outcomes that teacher exposure could plausibly affect, and both push toward the persistent, on-track subset of students — the subset for whom a marginal effect on college-going is least likely to appear.

STANDING AND WHAT IT SETS UP

As it stands, this is a solid but modest addition. It becomes the reference for a specific descriptive fact (no association between cumulative four-year matched-teacher exposure and college enrollment in NYC) and for a specific methodological warning (documented within-school sorting in high school matching). It does not become the reference for whether teacher diversity affects postsecondary access; the experimental and quasi-experimental work retains that role, and this paper does not contradict it so much as fail to reproduce it under a much weaker design in a different setting.

Its most useful legacy may be the question it opens rather than closes: why short-run outcomes (GPA, attendance) and the long-run outcome (enrollment) diverge. The paper offers structural-barrier and mediator explanations and tests neither. The authors note ongoing work on course-level matching, which is the right next step — subject, grade, and track are almost certainly where any real signal lives, and averaging over 27 teachers is likely to wash it out regardless of whether it exists.

One final note on framing for policy readers. The Implications section recommends recruitment of Asian American teachers on the basis of the Asian-student results, and suggests CUNY explore faculty-student matching. These recommendations rest on covariate-adjusted associations in a sample the paper has just shown to be non-randomly sorted, and on subgroup coefficients that are not consistently signed across specifications. A policy reader should treat them as hypotheses the paper motivates, not conclusions it supports.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper carries no data availability statement, no replication package, and no documented pathway for obtaining the NYCPS or NSC data it relies on, so nothing in the analysis is independently checkable except by a researcher who negotiates their own data agreement. More consequentially, the analytic sample is described three incompatible ways (159,832 students in the text, 153,081 in Tables 1a/1b, ~202,655 in Tables 3a and 8/9), the cohort window shifts between 2017-2020 in the text and 2016-2018 in several table titles and notes, and the central exposure measure is labeled 'teachers of color,' 'Asian, Black, and Latine teachers,' and 'URM teachers (Black, Latine, Native)' in three different places. Readers should treat the specification as transparent and the analytic dataset as not reconstructible from what is reported.

**Strengths:**

- The estimating equation is stated unambiguously enough to re-run: a student-level linear probability / OLS model with school fixed effects, cohort-of-graduation fixed effects, and standard errors clustered at the school where the student attended 12th grade. The clustering unit is named precisely, which is more than many descriptive papers do.
- The estimation software and commands are named specifically -- Stata, reghdfe for the high-dimensional fixed effects, mmqreg for the method-of-moments quantile regression (with a supporting citation to Rios-Avila et al.), and coefplot for the figures. This is unusually concrete for education research and lets a replicator match the estimator exactly, even if the dataset cannot be matched.
- Every main and appendix regression table reports the point estimate, a standard error in parentheses, the number of observations, the adjusted R-squared, and the number of clusters, column by column. The covariate vector is spelled out in full in each table note rather than referred to generically, so the right-hand side of each model is recoverable from the exhibits alone.
- Several sample-construction decisions are stated with explicit magnitudes rather than vaguely: multiracial and 'other' race students removed (0.9% and 1.4% in 2018), special education schools excluded (10,603 students, ~3% of high school students in 2018), multiracial (2.77%) and 'other' race (2.33%) teachers dropped. Reporting the size of each exclusion is good practice and lets a reader judge whether the exclusions could matter.
- The paper reports a real sensitivity architecture and describes it in enough operational detail to be re-run: with/without covariates in every column, with/without GPA and attendance as mediating controls (Tables A3-A4), lagged (grades 9-11) versus contemporaneous (9-12) versions of those controls, a single-school-attenders subsample (Table A5), quantile regressions, and two Delhommer-style sorting tests (Tables 11a-d and 12a-d).
- Funding sources (Walton Family Foundation, Chan Zuckerberg Initiative), a conflict-of-interest declaration, ORCID identifiers, and an acknowledgement naming NYCPS as the data provider are all present, so the provenance and sponsorship of the work are disclosable facts rather than guesses.

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data availability statement anywhere in the article, and no documented access pathway. The Acknowledgements thank NYCPS 'for providing access to the data' -- that is the entire account of how the data were obtained. No data-use agreement, no NYCPS research-request process, no application contact, no NSC StudentTracker research-service description, no restricted-file identifier. A would-be replicator is given no starting point at all beyond 'ask New York City.' There is also no IRB or human-subjects statement and no preregistration.
- No replication package, repository, DOI, or example/synthetic code is posted or referenced. Restricted data legitimately cannot be shared, but the do-files that build the analytic file and produce the tables face no such restriction, and none are deposited. One set of results -- the two-year and four-year enrollment models using the share of Black, Latine, and Native teachers as predictor -- is explicitly reported only as 'available upon request,' which by current journal-era norms is not a substitute for either a table or a deposit.
- The reported analytic sample is internally contradictory in a way that cannot be resolved from the text. The Methods section states 'Our final sample consisted of 159,832 students, with one observation per student for high school graduates in the years 2017-2020,' but that number appears nowhere else in the paper. Tables 1a and 1b report N = 153,081; Table 3a reports N = 202,655 for the whole sample; the main regressions run on 201,846-202,655 observations without covariates and ~201,071-201,286 with them. A replicator has no way to know which N is the target.
- The Table 1a/1b subgroup counts do not sum to their own reported total: 32,388 (Asian) + 42,211 (Black) + 57,098 (Latine) + 1,030 (Native) + 24,874 (White) = 157,601, against a stated 'All' column N of 153,081. Whichever number is wrong, the descriptive exposure distributions -- the exhibit a reader would use to gauge how much variation the key predictor actually has -- cannot be reconciled with themselves.
- The cohort window is inconsistent across the paper. The text, abstract, and every regression table note say graduating cohorts 2017-2020. But Table 1a is titled '2016-2017 and 2018-2019' and its note says 'We include all students who graduated from high school in the years 2016-2018'; Table 1b repeats this; Table 3a is titled 'For Cohorts Graduating Between 2016 and 2018.' The descriptive tables and the estimation tables therefore appear to describe different populations, and nothing in the paper says which labeling is correct.
- The central exposure variable is defined three incompatible ways. The Data section defines teachers of color as 'Asian American, Black, Latine, or Native American teachers,' then immediately says 'we carried out our analyses using only Black, Latine, or Native teachers.' Table 1b is titled 'Share of Teachers of Color' but its note describes 'the share of Asian, Black, and Latine teachers.' Tables 5, 7, and 9 label the regressor 'URM teachers.' Table 3a calls it 'Asian, Black, Latine Teacher Share.' Whether Asian teachers are inside or outside the measure changes what the abstract's 'proportion of teachers of color' claim means, and a replicator would have to guess.
- The construction of the match share is under-specified at the step that matters most. The paper builds indicators at the student-course-year level, tabulates 'the number of occurrences where a student had a teacher of the same race,' then divides 'by that student's total number of teachers in that year' -- a numerator counted over course-year observations against a denominator described as a teacher count. These differ whenever a teacher teaches a student more than one course. The four-year aggregate is then described only as 'the total proportion... across grades 9-12,' which could be the mean of four annual proportions or a single pooled ratio over all course-teacher observations; Table 3a's 'Total Teacher Count 26.96' hints at the pooled version, but it is never stated.
- It is never specified which courses and teachers enter the denominator. There is no statement about physical education, arts, advisory or homeroom, credit-recovery or online courses, or courses below some credit threshold; no statement about how co-taught sections are handled, which matters a great deal given that 19% of teachers in Table 2a hold Special Education licenses; and no statement about how the excluded multiracial and 'other'-race teachers (5.1% of the workforce) are treated -- dropped from the denominator entirely, or retained and counted as non-matches. That single choice moves every match share.
- The college enrollment outcome has no stated time window. It is described only as 'a binary indicator of whether a student enrolled in college.' Immediate fall enrollment, enrollment within a year, or ever-observed enrollment through the 2022 NSC pull are all consistent with the text and would produce materially different rates. The paper also states that 'approximately 70 percent of NYCPS students had postsecondary records in NSC data' while Table 3a reports 83% enrolled in college, and does not explain the gap, does not say whether a non-match in NSC is coded zero or missing, and does not address NSC directory-suppression or FERPA blocks, which are the standard threat to this outcome.
- The covariates are described as characteristics 'that were consistent over time for each student,' but poverty status, ELL status, and IEP status are all time-varying in NYCPS administrative files. No collapsing rule is given -- ever-flagged, ninth-grade value, modal value, twelfth-grade value -- and the choice affects both the covariate-adjusted columns (which is where nearly every headline result lives) and the sorting tests in Tables 12a-d, where these same flags are the outcomes of interest.
- The lagged control is described inconsistently across table notes: Tables 4, 5, 7, and 9 say the models include 'the average number of days of school attended in grades 9-11,' while Table 6 and Figure 1 say 'the average attendance rate in grades 9-11.' A count of days and a rate are different variables, and a replicator cannot tell which was actually in each model.
- Several numbers in the Results narration do not match the tables they describe. The text summarizing Table 3a reports White students at '0.47 versus 0.16' where the table shows .51 versus .16; describes students with more than a quarter matched teachers as 'less likely to be... Latine (0.36 versus 0.16 for the full sample)' where the table shows .12 versus .37 -- the two figures appear transposed; and gives poverty as '0.74 versus 0.83' where the table shows .75 and .85. These are the descriptive contrasts the sorting story rests on.
- The quantile-regression sensitivity analysis exists only as coefficient plots (Figure 1, Figures B1 and B2). No underlying point estimates, standard errors, or quantile-specific sample sizes are tabulated anywhere, so the claim that 'there are not statistically significant relationships with our outcomes in any quartile' is verifiable only by eyeballing error bars. The text also refers to 'Appendices B1 and B2' as if they were tables when they are figures.
- Small internal irregularities in the exhibits are left unexplained and complicate any attempt at an exact match. Cluster counts move with the covariate set (Table 4 all-students: 485 without covariates, 484 with) in a pattern consistent with reghdfe singleton-dropping that is never documented; in Table 5 the White columns show 390 clusters without covariates and 391 with, despite the sample shrinking from 31,940 to 31,789, which cannot happen under nested samples. Table 9 reports N = 31,9935 for one White column, and Table A1 an adjusted R-squared of '0337.'
- Tables 10, 11a-d, and 12a-d present coefficient/standard-error pairs without the parenthetical convention used elsewhere in the paper, and in Table 10 the second entry in several cells carries a negative sign. Combined with the text's report of a significant 'less competitive' coefficient (B = -0.0119, p < .001) whose value appears under a differently-labeled column, the selectivity results in particular are hard to read off the exhibit with confidence.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not treat any single sample size in this paper as the analytic N. Before citing the study, decide which population you think it describes: the 159,832 in the Methods text, the 153,081 in Tables 1a/1b, or the ~202,655 in Table 3a and the regressions. The regression tables are self-consistent around ~201,000-202,655, so that is the defensible reading of what was actually estimated -- but note that the descriptive exposure distributions in Tables 1a/1b (the basis for any claim about how much matched-teacher variation students experience) are drawn from a smaller and differently-labeled sample whose own subgroups sum to 157,601 rather than 153,081.
- Check the cohort window against the version of record before repeating the study's coverage claim. The text says graduating cohorts 2017-2020; Tables 1a, 1b, and 3a say 2016-2018 or 2016-17 through 2018-19. If you are citing this as four cohorts spanning the pre-pandemic through 2020 period, verify that with the authors -- the 2020 cohort's senior spring was disrupted by COVID school closures, and whether it is in or out of the descriptive tables materially affects the attendance-rate results in particular.
- Treat the 'teachers of color' results (Tables 5, 7, 9) as results about Black, Latine, and Native teachers, not about teachers of color inclusive of Asian teachers -- the Data section says the analyses used 'only Black, Latine, or Native teachers,' and the table stubs say 'URM teachers.' Read the abstract's statement that 'the proportion of teachers of color' was unrelated to college enrollment with that narrower definition in mind, and note the tension with Table 1b's note describing an Asian-inclusive share. Ask the authors which definition generated each exhibit before reusing these coefficients.
- Before comparing this study's exposure magnitudes to Delhommer (2022), Lindsay and Hart (2017), or Gershenson et al. (2022), recognize that the match share here is not comparably defined. Ask the authors four specific things: whether the numerator counts course-year observations or distinct teachers; whether the four-year share is a mean of annual shares or a pooled ratio; which course types (PE, arts, advisory, credit recovery) are in the denominator and how co-taught sections are counted; and whether the 5.1% of teachers dropped for multiracial/'other' race were removed from the denominator or retained as non-matches. Each answer changes the scale of the regressor, and every coefficient in the paper is per-unit-of-that-regressor.
- Request the college-enrollment definition before using the null result. 'Whether a student enrolled in college' with a 2022 NSC pull could be immediate fall enrollment or ever-enrollment, and the paper's own 70% NSC-coverage figure sits awkwardly against Table 3a's 83% enrollment rate. Ask specifically how non-matches to NSC were coded (zero versus dropped) and whether directory-suppressed records were addressed -- if non-matches are coded as non-enrollment and suppression correlates with school, the school fixed effects will absorb some of it but the outcome is still measured with race-correlated error.
- The specification itself is the most reproducible part of this paper and is worth re-running on other administrative data: student-level OLS/LPM, school and graduation-cohort fixed effects via reghdfe, clustered on twelfth-grade school, with gender, poverty, ELL, IEP, number of schools attended, and lagged (grades 9-11) GPA and attendance as controls. If you attempt this in another district, note that you will have to make the undocumented construction choices above yourself, so treat any divergence in magnitude as uninformative about replication failure until those choices are pinned down.
- Treat the quantile-regression sensitivity analysis as unverified. The point estimates exist only as plotted error bars in Figures 1, B1, and B2 -- no coefficients, standard errors, or quantile sample sizes are reported. If the null-across-quartiles finding is load-bearing for your reading of the paper, request the underlying estimates from the authors.
- Do not cite the two-year and four-year enrollment results using the Black/Latine/Native teacher share; the paper reports them only as 'available upon request.' Similarly, the college-selectivity findings in Table 10 should be checked against the typeset version of record before being quoted, since the standard errors are printed without the parenthetical convention used elsewhere and the text's reported 'less competitive' coefficient does not sit cleanly under that column.
- Reconcile the Results narration of Table 3a against the table itself before repeating the sorting descriptives. The text's White (0.47 vs 0.16), Latine (0.36 vs 0.16), and poverty (0.74 vs 0.83) contrasts do not match the table's .51/.16, .12/.37, and .75/.85 -- and the Latine pair appears transposed, which reverses the direction of the described contrast. The qualitative sorting story survives, but the specific figures should not be quoted from the prose.
- If you intend a full replication, the binding constraint is data access, and the paper gives you no route. Plan on approaching the NYCPS Research and Policy Support Group independently for the student, course, teacher, and attendance files and separately contracting with the National Student Clearinghouse for a StudentTracker research match; budget for the review timeline, and expect to negotiate the linkage yourself, since the paper does not describe how students were joined to teachers of record or what fraction of course records lacked a linkable teacher.
- Weight the paper's claim structure accordingly. The design logic, the direction of the sorting evidence, and the internal robustness pattern (results attenuating toward null when covariates or single-school samples are used) are visible and self-consistent in the exhibits and can be assessed on the page. The specific coefficient magnitudes -- the 4.6- and 3.64-point GPA associations, the two-percentage-point attendance figures, the one-percentage-point enrollment estimate -- are conditional on an exposure variable whose scale is not documented and a sample whose size the paper reports three ways, and should be cited as directional evidence rather than as effect sizes.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Assessed against journal-era norms for a published article, this paper's transparency is well below what a reader should now expect, and the shortfall is not primarily about the restricted data. There is no data availability statement of any kind. The only account of provenance is a line in the Acknowledgements thanking New York City Public Schools 'for providing access to the data' and naming two individuals. No data-use agreement is referenced, no NYCPS research-request process is described, no NSC StudentTracker service or contract is named, and there is no IRB or human-subjects statement and no preregistration. That NYCPS student-level administrative records cannot be posted publicly is entirely legitimate and should not count against the paper. What does count against it is that the paper documents no pathway by which anyone else could obtain equivalent access, which converts a restricted-data study into an effectively closed one. Nor is there any replication package, repository, or deposited code -- and the do-files that construct the analytic file and produce the tables carry no confidentiality restriction at all. One set of results, the two-year and four-year enrollment models using the Black/Latine/Native teacher share, is reported only as 'available upon request,' which by contemporary standards earns little credit.

The more serious problem is that the analytic sample cannot be identified from the paper, because the paper reports it three different ways. The Measuring Student Exposure section states flatly that 'Our final sample consisted of 159,832 students, with one observation per student for high school graduates in the years 2017-2020.' That figure appears nowhere else in the article. Tables 1a and 1b, which present the exposure distributions, report N = 153,081 -- and their own subgroup columns (32,388 Asian, 42,211 Black, 57,098 Latine, 1,030 Native, 24,874 White) sum to 157,601, so those tables are not internally consistent either. Table 3a reports a whole-sample N of 202,655, which is also the N in the uncontrolled columns of Tables 8 and 9, with the covariate-adjusted columns landing near 201,071. A replicator building toward this study has no target to hit. The regression exhibits are at least self-consistent with each other, which makes ~201,000-202,655 the defensible reading of what was estimated; but that leaves the descriptive exposure tables -- the exhibits a reader would use to judge how much identifying variation exists in the key regressor -- describing a different and unreconciled population.

The cohort window compounds this. The abstract, the Data section, and every regression table note specify graduating cohorts 2017 through 2020. Table 1a is titled 'Share of Ethnoracially Matched Teacher by Percentiles and Student Race 2016-2017 and 2018-2019' and its note reads 'We include all students who graduated from high school in the years 2016-2018.' Table 1b repeats the same note. Table 3a is titled 'For Cohorts Graduating Between 2016 and 2018.' Either the descriptive tables use a different window than the estimation tables, or the table titles and notes are stale from an earlier draft. Nothing in the paper resolves it, and the resolution matters substantively: the 2020 cohort's senior year was truncated by pandemic school closures, so whether that cohort is present bears directly on the average attendance rate and on the GPA measure.

The central predictor is where a replication would most obviously diverge. The measure is built as follows: an indicator at the student-course-year level for whether the course was taught by an ethnoracially matched teacher; a tabulation of 'the number of occurrences where a student had a teacher of the same race'; division 'by that student's total number of teachers in that year'; and then 'the total proportion of same-race teachers... across grades 9-12.' There are at least three undocumented choices packed into that sentence. First, the numerator is counted over course-year observations while the denominator is described as a count of teachers -- these coincide only if no teacher ever teaches the same student two courses, which is false in practice for math and English sequences and for special-education push-in. Second, the four-year aggregation could be the unweighted mean of four annual proportions or a single pooled ratio across all course-teacher observations; students with uneven course loads across grades get different values under the two rules. Table 3a's 'Total Teacher Count 26.96' and the text's 'Students had an average of 27 teachers across the four years' suggest a pooled count, but it is never said. Third, and most consequentially, nothing states which courses enter the denominator. Physical education, arts, advisory, homeroom, credit recovery, and online coursework are all plausibly in or out; the GPA measure explicitly excludes pass-fail courses, but whether the exposure denominator applies the same exclusion is not stated. Co-taught sections receive no treatment at all despite Table 2a showing that 19% of the matched teacher workforce holds a Special Education license -- a setting where two teachers of record per section is routine and where the handling choice would systematically shift match shares for exactly the IEP students whose sorting the paper highlights in Table 12b. And the 5.1% of teachers dropped as multiracial or 'other' race must land somewhere: removed from the denominator, or retained and counted as non-matches. Those two rules yield different exposure values for every student who had such a teacher. Every coefficient in the paper is expressed per one-unit change in this variable, so its undocumented scale propagates into every magnitude the paper reports.

The 'teachers of color' construct is defined inconsistently in a way that changes what the headline null result means. The Data section defines teachers of color as those identifying as 'Asian American, Black, Latine, or Native American,' and then states in the next clause that 'we carried out our analyses using only Black, Latine, or Native teachers, who were considered underrepresented in higher education.' Tables 5, 7, and 9 accordingly label the regressor 'URM teachers.' But Table 1b is titled 'Share of Teachers of Color Percentiles by Student Race' while its note describes 'the share of Asian, Black, and Latine teachers,' and Table 3a's stub reads 'Asian, Black, Latine Teacher Share.' Three definitions -- Asian-inclusive, Asian-exclusive, and Native-inclusive-but-Asian-exclusive -- circulate through the paper's exhibits. Since the abstract's second headline finding is that 'the proportion of teachers of color' was unrelated to college enrollment, and since Native teachers are only 0.4% of the workforce, the practical question is whether the roughly 9% of teachers who are Asian are inside or outside the estimated variable. A reader cannot tell, and neither could a replicator.

The college enrollment outcome carries no time window. It is defined only as 'a binary indicator of whether a student enrolled in college,' against NSC data cited to 2022. Immediate-fall enrollment, within-one-year enrollment, and ever-enrolled-through-2022 are all consistent with that sentence and would produce different rates and different coefficients. The paper also states that 'approximately 70 percent of NYCPS students had postsecondary records in NSC data' while Table 3a reports an enrollment rate of .83 -- reconcilable if the 70% figure covers all NYCPS students and the 83% covers graduates only, but the paper does not say so. Nothing addresses how NSC non-matches were coded, whether directory-suppressed records were handled, or what the linkage rate was. Since NSC coverage and suppression vary by institution type and correlate with student demographics, this is measurement error in the outcome that is potentially correlated with the regressor of interest, and it is entirely undocumented.

Covariate construction is similarly thin. The paper says the covariate vector comprises 'demographic characteristics and academic performance variables that were consistent over time for each student,' listing race, gender, IEP status, poverty, and ELL status. Poverty, ELL, and IEP status are all time-varying in NYCPS files, and the paper gives no rule for collapsing them to one value per student -- ever-flagged, ninth-grade, twelfth-grade, or modal. This matters twice over, because these same flags are the outcomes in the Table 12a-d sorting analyses that carry the paper's main interpretive claim. Meanwhile the lagged academic control is described as 'the average number of days of school attended in grades 9-11' in the notes to Tables 4, 5, 7, and 9 but as 'the average attendance rate in grades 9-11' in Table 6 and Figure 1 -- a count and a rate, used interchangeably in the documentation of the same model family.

On results reporting, the main tables do most of what they should: point estimates, standard errors in parentheses, N, adjusted R-squared, cluster counts, and explicit covariate lists, column by column. Two gaps stand out. First, the quantile-regression sensitivity analysis exists only as plotted coefficients (Figure 1, B1, B2); no estimates, standard errors, or quantile sample sizes appear anywhere, so the claim of no significant relationships in any quartile is checkable only by reading error bars off a chart, and the text compounds the confusion by referring to 'Appendices B1 and B2' as though they were tables. Second, Tables 10 through 12 abandon the parenthetical standard-error convention used elsewhere, and in Table 10 several of the second entries carry negative signs; combined with the text's report of a significant 'less competitive' coefficient of -0.0119 whose value appears under a differently labeled column in the extracted table, the college-selectivity results are the least legible in the paper. I hold that observation more loosely than the others, since I am reading a text extraction of a two-column typeset PDF and some column alignment may be an artifact; a reader should check that exhibit in the version of record rather than take my reading of it.

Several smaller irregularities are worth noting because they signal that the exhibits did not receive a final numerical proofread, which bears on how much a reader should trust exact figures. Cluster counts change with the covariate set in a pattern consistent with reghdfe dropping singletons, which is never documented; but in Table 5 the White columns report 390 clusters without covariates and 391 with, while the sample falls from 31,940 to 31,789, which cannot occur under nested samples. Table 9 reports N = 31,9935. Table A1 reports an adjusted R-squared of '0337.' And the Results narration of Table 3a misstates three of its own descriptive contrasts: White as 0.47 versus the table's .51, poverty as 0.74/0.83 versus the table's .75/.85, and Latine as '0.36 versus 0.16' where the table shows .12 in the matched column against .37 in the full sample -- an apparent transposition that reverses the direction of the described difference. The qualitative sorting story survives all of this, but a reader should quote from the tables rather than the prose.

Weighing this: the design and estimator are genuinely well documented -- reghdfe, mmqreg, school and cohort fixed effects, clustering on twelfth-grade school, covariate lists in every note. Someone with independent NYCPS and NSC access could re-implement the specification with confidence. What they could not do is verify they had built the same analytic dataset, because the paper reports its sample three ways, labels its cohorts two ways, and defines its central exposure variable at a level of detail that leaves at least four consequential construction choices to the replicator's discretion. That is why this lands at 'weak' rather than 'adequate': the obstruction is not the restricted data, which is excusable, but the documentation of sample and variable construction, which was fully within the authors' control. It is not 'insufficient' -- the design is intelligible, the sensitivity architecture is described, the exhibits carry uncertainty and sample sizes, and a determined replicator has a real starting point. Readers should feel comfortable citing the paper's directional pattern and its sorting evidence, and should treat its specific magnitudes as provisional pending clarification from the authors.
